en: Śaṃkara (author): Kaṭhopaniṣadbhāṣya;
Kaṭhopaniṣad.
Oṃ!
May he protect us both; may he nourish us both; may we perform our work with vigor together.
May our study be brilliant; may we never harbor ill will toward one another.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Oṃ. Salutations to the Blessed One, Vaivasvata, Death, the teacher of the knowledge of Brahman, and to Naciketas.
Now, for the purpose of easily awakening the meaning of the chapters (vallīs) of the Kaṭhaka Upaniṣad, this brief commentary is commenced.
This word "Upaniṣad" is a form derived from the root *sad*, meaning "to dissolve," "to go," or "to perish," preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *ni*, and ending in the suffix *kvip*.
And by the word *upaniṣad*, the knowledge (*vidyā*) concerning the reality to be known—which is the subject matter to be expounded in the text intended for exposition—is denoted.
But by what etymological connection is knowledge expressed by the word *upaniṣad*? It is said:
those seekers of liberation who, being free from thirst for seen and revealed objects, [approach] that which is denoted by the word *upaniṣad* and possesses the characteristics to be described...

Having approached and resorted to knowledge, those who cultivate it with certainty through steadfast devotion—because of the dissolution, destruction, and eradication of ignorance and the other seeds of saṃsāra—it is called the *vidyopaniṣad* in this sense.
And so he will say: "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death" (KaU 3.15).

Alternatively, it is called the *Brahmavidyopaniṣad* because it leads those seeking liberation—possessing the previously mentioned qualifications—to the Supreme Brahman; thus, it is designated as such through its connection with being the "conveyor to Brahman.

And so it will be stated: "Having reached Brahman, he became free from passion and free from death" (KaU 3.18). This refers to the knowledge concerning the fire that is the source of the worlds and born of Brahman (*brahmajajña*), which was sought as the second boon.

Because it brings about the attainment of the fruit of the heavenly world, and because it causes the exhaustion—by inducing slackening—of the multitude of afflictions such as dwelling in the womb, birth, and old age that recur repeatedly in other worlds, the knowledge of fire (*agnividyā*) is also called an *upaniṣad* due to its connection with the meaning of the verbal root [to sit down near].
And so he will say: "They partake of immortality in the heavenly world" (KaU 1.13), and so forth.
But surely students also refer to the book itself by the word "Upaniṣad," as in "We study the Upaniṣad" and "We teach the Upaniṣad.
This is not a fault.

Because the meaning of the verbal root *sad*— namely, the dissolution of the causes of saṃsāra such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth— is impossible in the case of a mere book but possible in the case of knowledge (*vidyā*),
and because even a book may be designated by that term insofar as it has that [knowledge] as its purpose (just as clarified butter is called "life" [*āyuḥ*]),
therefore the word *upaniṣad* applies to knowledge in its primary sense.
In the text, however, it says "through devotion.
Thus, by the very etymological definition of *upaniṣad*, the qualified candidate for knowledge (*vidyā*) has been stated;
and the specific object of that knowledge has also been stated as the Supreme Brahman, which is one's own inner self (*pratyagātman*).
The purpose (*prayojana*) of this Upaniṣad is the absolute cessation of saṃsāra, characterized by the attainment of Brahman.
The relationship (*sambandha*) has likewise been stated as being with such a purpose.

Therefore, these chapters (*vallīs*), which possess a specific qualification, subject matter, purpose, and relationship, serve to illuminate—like a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of the hand—the knowledge (*vidyā*) that possesses the aforementioned qualification, subject matter, purpose, and relationship.
Since these [passages] exist, we shall explain them according to our inspiration: "Oṃ!
Uśanas Vājaśravasa indeed gave away all his possessions."
He had a son named Naciketas.
In this context, the narrative is for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*).
The particles *u* and *ha vai* serve to recall the events that have already occurred.
One whose *vāja*—meaning food—and *śravaḥ*—meaning fame resulting from the giving of that [food] and so forth—is *vājaśravas*.
Or [the name] is based on conventional usage;
he was the offspring of Vājaśravas. It is said that he performed the Viśvajit sacrifice, the Sarvamedha, desiring its fruit.
In that sacrifice, he gave away all his possessions—his entire wealth.
That sacrificer had, it is said, a son named Naciketas who was ill-disposed.

While he was still a youth and the sacrificial gifts were being led away, faith entered him; he reflected: KaU 1.2.1–2: "While he was still a youth and the sacrificial gifts were being led away, faith entered him; he reflected."

While that boy Naciketas was still in his early youth, a child who had not yet attained the capacity for procreation, faith—consisting of a conviction in the scriptures and a sense of devotion—entered him, impelled by his father’s desire for his welfare.

At what time did this occur? The text says: while the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) were being led away and distributed in portions to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the members of the assembly (*sadasya*), and while the cows intended as the fee were being led away; at that time, Naciketas, possessed by that faith, reflected thus.
Those who give such cows go to those worlds known as "Joyless," where the water has been drunk, the grass eaten, the milk milked out, and the senses are gone. (KaU 1.3)
How so? It is said: by the words "having drunk water" and so forth, the cows intended for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) are qualified.
Those by whom water has been drunk are "those who have drunk water" (*pītodakāḥ*).
Those by whom grass has been eaten—that is, consumed—are "those who have eaten grass" (*jagdhatṛṇāḥ*).
"Dugdhadohāḥ" means those whose milk, known as "doha," has been milked out;
the meaning is that they are cows that are barren, incapable of reproduction, aged, and fruitless.

He who gives such cows to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) with the intention of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)—being "anandaḥ," meaning joyless, unhappy, or miserable—goes to those worlds which bear such names. That sacrificer goes to those worlds.
He said to his father, "Father, to whom will you give me? A second time and a third time he asked this, and his father said to him, "I give you to Death."

Thus, thinking, "I must, as a son, avert this undesirable result for my father caused by the failure of the sacrifice—even by the gift of myself—thereby ensuring the completion of the rite," he approached his father and said to him: "O father, dear one, to which specific officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) will you give me as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)? That is to say, whom will you bestow upon me?"
Even though he was being ignored by his parents when he had spoken thus, he said a second and even a third time, "To whom will you give me? To whom will you give me?
Becoming angry because this was not the nature of a prince, his father said to that son, "I give you to Death, to Vaivasvata."
"I go as the first among many; I go as the middlemost among many.
What indeed is this duty of Yama that he will perform through me today? (KaU 1.5)
Having been addressed thus, the son lamented in private.
How so? It is said: "Among many disciples or sons, I go as the foremost, meaning I proceed with the primary conduct of a disciple or similar role;
and among many middling ones, I go as a middling one, proceeding with middling conduct."
Never, even at the lowest point,
did my father say to me— his son endowed with such distinguished qualities— “I give you to death” (KaU 1.4).
"What purpose for Yama will he accomplish with me given by him; what task must he perform today?
Surely his father spoke out of the power of anger, regardless of any actual need.
Nevertheless, [the son thought], "Let not the word of my father be false. (KaU Bh 1.5)
Thinking thus, and preceded by lamentation, he said to his father who was overcome with grief: "What have I said?
"Observe how it was for those of old, and observe likewise for those of later times.
Like grain, a mortal ripens; like grain, he is born again. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.6)
Contemplate and reflect upon them in due order, in whatever manner and by whatever means your ancestors—the fathers, grandfathers, and so forth—conducted themselves in the past;
having seen their conduct, you ought to abide by it. Likewise, observe and reflect upon those other virtuous people who are living now and how they conduct themselves.
Neither for them does there exist a practice of falsehood, whether past or present;
rather, it is the opposite of that, and the practice of the unrighteous is the commission of falsehood.
Furthermore, by committing what is false, no one becomes free from old age and death.
Since a mortal man ripens like grain— withering and dying— and having died, he is born again and appears like grain, then in this impermanent world of living beings, what is the use of falsehood?
Protect your own truth.
"Send me to Yama"—this is the intended meaning.
The Vaiśvānara fire enters the house as a Brāhmaṇa guest;
they perform this pacification for him: "O Vaivasvata, take water! (KaU 1.7).
Thus addressed, his father sent him forth for the sake of proving his own truthfulness.
He went to the abode of Yama and stayed there for three nights while Yama was away.
When Yama had returned from his absence, the ministers or the wife said to him, awakening him: "The Brahmin guest, being truly Vaiśvānara Agni himself, enters the house as if burning it."

Since virtuous people perform this pacification— characterized by the offering of water for the feet, a seat, and so forth— for a guest, as if to quench the burning of a fire, therefore, O Vaivasvata, bring, bring water for Naciketas for the purpose of washing his feet;
for it is heard that there is sin in failing to do so.

Hope and expectation, social intercourse and pleasant speech, the merit of sacrifices and charitable works, as well as sons and cattle—all these he takes away from the man of small intelligence in whose house a Brahmin dwells without eating. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.8)

*Āśāpratīkṣa*: *Āśā* (hope) is the longing for a desired object that is not yet known to be attainable; *pratīkṣā* (waiting) is the waiting for an object already known to be attainable; these two are *āśāpratīkṣe*.
"Saṅgata" is the fruit born from association with the virtuous;
"sūnṛtā" refers to pleasant speech, as well as that which arises from it;
and "iṣṭāpūrta" refers to the fruit born of sacrifice (*iṣṭa*).

"Pūrtam" refers to the fruit born of ritual actions such as the establishment of gardens and so forth; "putrapaśūn" means sons and cattle. All this, as described, he "vṛṅkte"—that is, he avoids and destroys—the man of "alpamedhasaḥ," meaning one of small intellect or limited wisdom.
The meaning is that since a Brahmin who does not eat— that is, one who does not partake of food— dwells in one's house, therefore a guest must not be neglected under any circumstances whatsoever.

"Since for three nights you have dwelt in my house as a guest, O Brahmin, without eating and worthy of honor—homage be to you, O Brahmin, and may it be well with me; therefore, choose three boons in return. (KaU 1.9)

Thus addressed, Death approached Naciketas and, preceded by worship, said: "O Brahmin, since you, as my guest, have stayed for three nights in my house without eating— being one worthy of honor and deserving of salutation—
therefore, let there be salutation unto you."
"O Brahmin, may there be well-being; may prosperity be mine.

Therefore, regarding the fault arising from your dwelling in my house due to fasting—if, through the pacification of that [fault] and by your favor, all may be well for me, nevertheless, it is for the sake of further propitiating you..."
"Having fasted for each single night, choose three boons; pray for whatever specific desired objects you wish from me."
O Death, may Gautama be of peaceful resolve, well-disposed, and free from anger toward me; may he speak to me with a friendly mind when sent by you. This first of three boons I choose. (KaU 1.10)

But Naciketas said: "O Death, if my father Gautama, having reached you, should have his intentions pacified—meaning that his resolve toward me is stilled—and should think, 'What indeed will he do with me as his son? then, O Death, let him be one whose intentions are pacified, who is well-disposed and serene in mind, and who is free from anger and resentment toward me."
Furthermore, let him whom you have sent forth, released, and dispatched toward my home, greet me with confidence and having regained his memory;
that is to say, let him recognize me, thinking, "This is indeed that son of mine who has returned.
This is the purpose for which I choose, I pray for, the first among the three boons—the very first boon—which is the pleasing of my father.
As before, Auddālaki Āruṇi shall become renowned, sent forth by me;
with his anger gone, he will sleep peacefully through the nights, having seen you released from the jaws of Death.

Death said: "Just as your intellect was previously endowed with affection for him before, so shall your father be endowed with love and be well-disposed toward you. Thus being convinced, Uddālaka Āruṇi—the son of Uddālaka (Auddālaki), the descendant of Aruṇa (Āruṇi), or one belonging to two lineages—being permitted and authorized by me, shall [live] through the subsequent nights as well."

Having seen you, his son, released from the jaws of death—that is, from the domain of death—he becomes happy, sleeps with a serene mind, and is free from mental distress and free from anger. (KaU Bh 1.11)

In the heavenly world there is no fear whatsoever; there you do not tremble at old age. Having crossed over both hunger and thirst, and having gone beyond sorrow, one rejoices in the heavenly world. (KaU 1.12)
Naciketas said: "In the heavenly world, there is not even the slightest fear caused by disease or other such things;
nor, O Death, do you have power there suddenly.
Therefore, unlike in this world, no one there fears you, for they are free from old age."

Moreover, having crossed over both hunger and thirst, having passed beyond sorrow—he being one who has transcended sorrow—freed from mental suffering, he rejoices and exults in the divine world of heaven.
"O Death, you know that fire which leads to heaven; tell it to me, who am full of faith.
Those who attain the world of heaven partake in immortality; this I choose as my second boon. (KaU 1.13)
The meaning is this: you, O Death, know—recollect, that is, remember—the *svargya* fire, which is the means for attaining the heavenly world characterized by such qualities.

Therefore, O Death, tell it, explain it to me, who am full of faith, possessed of devotion, and seeking heaven. By means of which piled fire the sacrificers—who possess the heavenly world (*svargalokāḥ*)—attain immortality, the state of being deathless.
They partake of and attain divinity; this very knowledge of Agni I choose with my second boon.
I declare this to you; understand it from me, O Naciketas, for I know the heavenly Agni.
Know that he is the attainment of the infinite world and the final support, hidden within the secret cave of the heart.

This is the promise of Death: "I shall declare to you—that which you have requested—listen to that from my words, understanding it with a one-pointed mind. O Naciketas, knowing well Agni who is conducive to heaven (*svargya*), that is, beneficial for heaven and the means to attain heaven—I [myself] am the one who has known him. This is the meaning.
"I shall proclaim; understand that"—this statement is for the purpose of concentrating the intellect of the disciple.
Now he praises Agni: "Infinite" means the means for attaining the worlds, namely the attainment of the fruit of the heavenly world (*svargaloka*).

Furthermore, know—that is, understand—this very Agni whom I am describing as the "foundation," the support of the universe in the form of Virāj; know him as "deposited," situated, established within the "cave," that is, seated in the intellect of the wise.
This is the meaning. (KaU Bh 1.14)
He told him about that Agni who is the beginning of the worlds—what bricks he consists of, how many there are, and how they are arranged;
and he (the son) replied to that exactly as it was told. Then Death, being pleased, spoke again to him.
This is the statement of the Śruti:

Mṛtyu spoke—that is, he said—to Naciketas, for him, about that Agni who is the subject under discussion and was requested by Naciketas, namely the "beginning of the worlds," the first [Agni] because he is bodiless;
and furthermore, [he spoke of] those bricks which are to be piled up in their own form.
The meaning is that he stated everything— whether by way of number, or how the fire-altar is piled up, or in whatever manner it is constructed.
And Naciketas, for his part, replied to that which was spoken by Death exactly as it was, having understood it through conviction and having repeated it word for word.
Then, being pleased by his repetition [of the mantra], Death spoke once more, desiring to grant another boon besides the three boons [already requested].
Being pleased, the Great-Souled One said to him: "I grant you yet another boon here today:
this fire shall be known by your very name; and take this *sṛṅkā* of manifold forms. (KaU 1.16)

How did he speak to that Naciketas? Seeing the fitness of his disciple, being pleased—experiencing joy—the Great-Souled One, whose intellect was not petty, said: "I shall now grant you, once again, a fourth boon as a cause for my pleasure."
This fire which I am describing shall become renowned by your very name, Naciketas.
Furthermore, accept—take possession of—this garland made of jewels, resounding with sound, multiform, and variegated;
or rather, accept this blameless course consisting of ritual action.
The meaning is: accept that there is yet another consciousness of karma as well, because it serves as the cause for manifold fruits.
Again, he speaks specifically in praise of action:
"One who has thrice kindled the *nāciketa* fire, having attained union by means of the three, and being a performer of the threefold duty, crosses over birth and death;
having known and realized the adorable God who is born of Brahman and is knowledge itself, he attains this ultimate peace. (KaU 1.17)
*Triṇāciketa*: one by whom the *nāciketa* fire has been piled three times is *triṇāciketa*; or, he is one who possesses the knowledge of that, the study of that, and the performance of that.
"Having attained the union" (*etya sandhim*) means having properly attained the connection—the bond consisting of the instruction of mother, father, and teacher.
For that is understood from another Vedic text to be the cause of authority, as in: "He who has a mother, who has a father... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2), and so forth.

Whether by means of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the teachings of the cultured, or by means of perception, inference, and scripture— for from these, purification is directly perceived— he who performs the three duties, the performer of sacrifice, study, and charity, crosses over and transcends birth and death.
Moreover, "born from Brahman" (brahmajajña) means one born from Brahman, that is, Hiraṇyagarbha;
and since he is both born from Brahman and a knower (jña), he is called "born from Brahman and a knower" (brahmajajña)—for he is indeed omniscient.
Having known that God—who is radiant with qualities such as knowledge and who is worthy of praise—from the scriptures, [one should worship Him].
Having discerned and seen this peace—cessation which is directly perceived by one's own intellect—one attains it, reaching it with excellence through the complete realization of the self-nature.
The meaning is that one attains the state of Vairāja by means of the practice of the combination of knowledge and action. (KaUBh 1.17)

Now he concludes the fruit of the piling of the fire-altar and the section itself: "O Triṇāciketa, having known this triad, whoever, knowing thus, piles the Nāciketa fire—having cast off the bonds of death before him, he who has transcended sorrow rejoices in the heavenly world. (KaU 1.18)

The one who has thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire— having known and understood this triad as described in the verse, "What bricks, how many, or how [they are placed]" (KaU 1.15)— and who, knowing the fire in this way as the nature of the Self, performs and completes the Nāciketa sacrificial rite (*kratu*), casts away before him, that is, first of all, the bonds of death characterized by unrighteousness, ignorance, passion, hatred, and so forth.

The meaning is "until the fall of the body. Having cast off [grief] and abandoned it, having transcended sorrow and being freed from mental sufferings, he rejoices in the world of heaven in the Vairāja realm through the realization of the true nature of the Virāj Self.
This is that heavenly Agni Naciketas which you chose with your second boon.
People will call this very Agni by your name; choose, O Naciketas, a third boon.
"This Agni, O Naciketas, is the boon for you—
this Agni which is conducive to heaven and the means for attaining heaven, which you requested as a boon with your second choice;
that Agni, the boon, has been granted"— thus ends the statement.
Furthermore, people shall call this fire by your very name— “the fire of [such-and-such] a person”—
this is the fourth boon granted by me, being pleased. O Naciketas, choose a third boon.
For the intention is this: "In that case, indeed, I am one who owes a debt. (KaU Bh 1.19)

For this much alone is to be understood from the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas concerning the meaning of injunctions and prohibitions— that is, the reality indicated by the two types of exhortations (*vara*), and not the knowledge of the true nature of the subject matter of the Self’s reality.

Therefore, for the purpose of removing that innate ignorance— which is the seed of transmigratory existence, which has as its object the domain of injunctions and prohibitions, and which is characterized by the superimposition of action, factors of action, and results upon the Self— there must arise the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, which is the opposite of that [ignorance] and is devoid of the characteristics of the superimposition of action, factors of action, and results.
The purpose of ultimate liberation (*atyantika-niḥśreyasa*) must be stated; therefore, the subsequent portion of the text begins.

This very point—that even by obtaining the second boon one has not yet accomplished one's purpose—is elaborated upon through a narrative concerning the third boon, namely that self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) is its scope:
"Regarding this doubt concerning a man who has died, some say 'he exists' and others say 'he does not exist.'"
Instructed by you, may I know this; this is the third of the boons.

Since one who has become detached from the aforementioned sphere of action, characterized by the relationship of means and ends and subject to impermanence, is qualified for the knowledge of the Self, an inducement is made through the mention of sons and other things in order to disparage that [sphere of action].
Being thus addressed—[by Yama] saying, "Naciketas, choose a third boon"—Naciketas said: "This doubt, this uncertainty, regarding a man who has passed away, who has died..."
"Some maintain that there exists a self distinct from the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, which is connected to another body; some say that such a self does not exist;
and others say that no such entity exists at all."
Therefore, for us, there is no definitive knowledge through either perception or inference.
Since the supreme human goal depends upon this knowledge, may I understand this science; instructed and informed by you, let me know it.
This is the third of the boons that remains.
To examine whether or not he is entirely worthy of the knowledge of the Self, which is the means for attaining the supreme good, [Naciketas] says:
"Even the gods had doubts about this in the past; for this dharma is not easily understood, being subtle.
Choose another boon, O Naciketas; do not press me [so], let go of this one. (KaU 1.21)
Even by the gods, there was formerly deliberated upon and doubted this very matter;
for it is not easily known—even though heard repeatedly—by ordinary people, since this subtle phenomenon called the Self is atomic.
Therefore, O Naciketas, choose another boon, one that has a visible fruit.
"Do not obstruct me; do not act like a creditor toward a debtor who has failed to pay.
Grant him his release; let go of this boon directed against me."
Thus addressed, Naciketas said: "Even the gods, it is said, have doubted this; and you, O Death, say that it is not easily understood.
A speaker of this [teaching] like you is not to be found elsewhere, nor is there any other boon equal to this. (KaU 1.22)

We have heard from you yourself that even the gods were, it is said, filled with doubt regarding this very matter. And since you, O Death, tell us that the true nature of the self is not easily understood, therefore, because it cannot be spoken by even the wise, no other speaker of this Dharma equal to you is to be found even when sought; yet this boon is the cause for attaining the supreme good.
Therefore, there is no other boon equal to or similar to this;
the intention is that everything else is inferior because its fruit is impermanent.
Even though he was addressed thus, Death spoke again, seeking to entice him:

"Choose many sons and grandsons with lives of a hundred years; choose numerous cattle, elephants, gold, and horses. Choose a vast estate of land, and live yourself as many autumns as you desire. (KaU 1.23)
Choose sons and grandsons who live for a hundred years— that is, those whose lifespans extend for a hundred years; furthermore, choose many cattle characterized by cows and the like,
as well as elephants and gold (the term *hastihiraṇyam* meaning both the elephant and the gold), and horses.
Furthermore, choose the great, vast domain, the support, the circle, and the sovereignty of the earth;

moreover, all this is useless if you yourself are short-lived—therefore he says: "And you yourself live, maintain the body with its full complement of sense-faculties for as many autumns, for as many years as you wish to live."
If you consider this equal [to what I have offered], choose a boon—wealth and long life;
O Naciketas, be established upon great earth, and I shall make you a partaker of all desires. (KaU 1.24)

If you consider this to be equal to, or even similar to, what has been taught here, then choose another boon as well. Furthermore, choose abundant wealth—gold, jewels, and the like—and long life along with that wealth. In short, O Naciketas, become a king upon the great earth; rule over a vast domain.
Moreover, I make you a partaker of desires—both divine and human—a recipient of desires, one worthy of desires;
for I am the God whose resolve is ever true.
"Whatever desires are difficult to obtain in the world of mortals, ask for all those desires according to your wish!
These beautiful women, with chariots and musical instruments—such as these are not to be obtained by men;
enjoy them with these who have been given to you by me, O Naciketas; do not ask about death. (KaU 1.25)

Whatever desires are to be prayed for and difficult to obtain in the world of mortals— pray for all those desires according to your will and inclination; moreover, these divine apsarases are called *rāmāḥ* because they delight men.
Those which exist together with chariots are "with chariots" (sarathāḥ); likewise, those with musical instruments and with musical accompaniment—
such as these, of this kind, cannot indeed be obtained or attained by human beings, such as ourselves, without our favor.
"With these female attendants given by me—bestowed by me—serve yourself;
that is to say, have them perform for you services such as washing your feet.

O Naciketas, do not ask about death—that question concerning death which is like an examination of a crow's teeth, asking whether there is or is not an existence after one has passed away. You ought not to ask thus.
Though thus tempted, Naciketas remained unshakable like a great lake and said:
"O Death, the very next day belongs to a mortal; this [world] wears away the vigor of all the senses.
Even the entirety of life is indeed brief; your horses, your dancing, and your singing are for you alone. (KaU 1.26)
Those objects of enjoyment which you have proposed, whose very existence is doubted—whether they will exist tomorrow or whether they will not exist at all—are called *śvobhāvāḥ*.

Furthermore, O Death, the ender of mortals, these enjoyments such as celestial nymphs (*apsarasaḥ*) and the like waste away and diminish that vigor of all the senses; they lead only to misfortune because they cause the destruction of virtue, energy, wisdom, splendor, fame, and so forth.
Furthermore, listen regarding that long life which you wish to bestow:
even the entire lifespan of Brahmā is but short; how much more so the long life of those such as ourselves?
Therefore, let your horses, chariots, and so forth remain yours, as well as your dancing and singing.
A man cannot be satisfied with wealth; we would have obtained wealth had we seen you [before].
We shall live as long as you rule, but that alone is the boon to be chosen by me.
Moreover, a human being cannot be satisfied by abundant wealth;

for in this world, the acquisition of wealth has never been seen to bring satisfaction to anyone. Even if we were to have a thirst for wealth—thinking "we shall obtain it," "we shall acquire it"—we would have seen you, O You, had we truly beheld you.
Our very life shall be the same; we shall live as long as you rule in the realm of Yama—when you are the sovereign and the lord.
For how could a mortal, having encountered you, have but meager wealth and short life?
But that alone is the boon to be chosen by me, which is the self-knowledge [of Brahman].

Having approached those who do not age and are immortal, what mortal, subject to decay and dwelling in a lowly state, would take pleasure—even while knowing better—in contemplating the colors, pleasures, and delights of this exceedingly long life? (KaU 1.28)
Since he knows and perceives from those who do not age— that is, who have not reached the decay of age and are immortal— a superior further purpose to be attained by approaching and going to them,

while he himself is aging, mortal, subject to old age and death, and situated below (kvadhaḥsthaḥ)— *kuḥ* being the earth, which is "below" in relation to the intermediate space and other worlds— upon that [earth]...
"Abiding"—how is it that one who stands thus [in the Self], while situated below, chooses such unstable things as sons, wealth, and so forth, which are sought after by the undiscriminating?
Or there is an alternative reading: "kva tadāsthaḥ.
In this case, the construction of the words is as follows: he whose *āsthā*—his abiding, his persistence, his application of intent—is toward those things such as sons and so forth, is "tadāsthaḥ."
Desiring to attain an even greater human goal, though it be difficult to reach, where could one have any attachment?
The meaning is that no one who knows its worthlessness would seek it.
For everyone in the world desires only to rise higher and higher; therefore, I am not to be enticed by the greed for sons, wealth, and the like.

Moreover, reflecting upon and examining the pleasures of color and delight headed by the Apsarases as being unstable in nature, what discerning person would take pleasure in a life that is so exceedingly long?
O Death, tell us that about which they have doubts regarding the great hereafter;
this boon which has entered into the secret—other than that, Naciketas chooses nothing else.
Thus ends the first chapter (vallī) in the Kaṭhaka Upaniṣad. // 1 //

Therefore, setting aside the temptation of impermanent desires which I have requested— that regarding which this ghost is in doubt, doubting in such a manner as "it exists" or "it does not exist"— O Death, tell us, declare to us that definitive knowledge concerning the great matter of the hereafter, the world beyond.
What more need be said?

Naciketas does not choose—even in his mind—any other boon sought by the undiscriminating, which concerns impermanent objects, than this boon concerning the Self that has been presented, which is hidden, profound, and difficult to discern, having reached and entered into it; such is the statement of the Śruti.
Thus ends the commentary on the first Vallī of the Kaṭhavallī. // 1 //
Now begins the second chapter (vallī).
Having examined the disciple and understood his fitness for knowledge, [the Teacher] said:
"The higher good is one thing, and the pleasant is indeed another; these two, having different aims, bind a person."
Of these two, for him who takes up the better, it becomes good; but he who chooses the pleasant falls away from his true purpose.
The higher good (*śreyaḥ*) is one thing, and likewise the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*) is another; moreover, the pleasant (*preyaḥ*), that which is more dear, is yet another.
These two—the pleasant and the higher good—having different meanings and distinct purposes, bind the person who is qualified by his caste, stage of life, and so forth.
Every person is impelled by these two, namely knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), as duties to be performed by the self.
For a person seeking prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and immortality (*amṛtatva*) engages in the pursuit of either the beneficial (*śreyas*) or the pleasant (*preyas*);
therefore, every person is said to be "cognizant" (*buddha*) by virtue of having understood these two as ends to be pursued and duties to be performed.

Although these two— knowledge and ignorance— are contradictory because they relate to the goals of different individuals and cannot be practiced simultaneously by a single person without abandoning one or the other, it is "good," "excellent," and "auspicious" for one who, having abandoned the form of ignorance, takes up and adopts only that which is beneficial;
whereas the deluded person of limited vision, being deprived, is separated from his goal— that is to say, he falls away from the eternal, ultimate purpose.
Who is this person who chooses—that is, accepts—the more pleasant? This is what is meant. (KaU Bh 2.1)
Both the beneficial and the pleasant approach a person; the wise man, having circled around both, discriminates between them.
For the wise man chooses the beneficial over the pleasant, while the dull-witted man chooses the pleasant for the sake of acquisition and security.
If both are within a person's own power to accomplish, why is it said that the world for the most part chooses only the pleasant? It is true that they are within one's power;

nevertheless, because their means and results are difficult for those of dull intellect to distinguish, both the beneficial (*śreyas*) and the pleasant (*preyas*) reach the human being as if they were intermingled.

Therefore, like a swan separating milk from water, the wise and steadfast person, having thoroughly examined and fully understood those two objects— the beneficial (*śreyaḥ*) and the pleasant (*preyaḥ*)— discriminates between them by weighing their relative importance and separates them.
Having thus discriminated, he indeed chooses only the beneficial, because it is more worthy than the pleasant.
Who is that wise one?

On the other hand, he who is dull-witted and of little intelligence, being incapable of discriminating between the real and the unreal, chooses that which is dear—characterized by cattle, sons, and so forth—for the sake of *yogakṣema*, meaning for the sake of acquisition and preservation, specifically for the purpose of nourishing and protecting the body and such things. (KaU Bh 2.2.1, 2.2)
O Naciketas, though you meditated upon dear and pleasant objects of desire, you have renounced them;
you have not attained this bait consisting of wealth, in which many men sink. (KaU 2.3)

Yet you, even though repeatedly enticed by me and dwelling upon your dear sons and other loved ones, as well as desirable objects characterized by celestial nymphs and the like, contemplated their defects— such as impermanence and lack of substance— and, O Naciketas, you cast them aside, rejected, and abandoned them; oh, how great is your wisdom!
You have not attained this auspicious path, but rather that contemptible way frequented by foolish people, which consists primarily of wealth and riches;
on that path many, indeed countless, foolish men sink and perish. (KaU 2.3)
Far apart and leading in opposite directions are these two, known as ignorance and knowledge.
I consider you, Naciketas, to be one who desires knowledge; indeed, many desires did not distract you. (KaU 2.4)
Regarding the statement, "Of these two, it is better for one who chooses the higher; he who chooses the pleasant falls away from his true purpose" (KaU 2.1), why is that?

Because these two are far apart—separated by a vast distance, being diametrically opposed and consisting of discernment and non-discernment respectively, like darkness and light—they move in different directions (*viṣūcī*) and have distinct results.
This refers to [their] being the causes of bondage in saṃsāra and liberation, respectively.

Who are they? It is said: that which is ignorance regarding what is dear (preyas) and knowledge regarding what is good (śreyas), when these have been discerned, fully understood, and realized by the wise—of those two, I consider you, Naciketas, to be one who desires knowledge, a seeker of knowledge.

Why? Because even though there were many desires—such as those for celestial nymphs—that entice the intellect of the ignorant, they did not cause you to crave them nor did they create a separation from the path to the highest good by fulfilling your longing for personal enjoyment;
therefore, my intention is that I consider you a seeker of knowledge and a vessel for the highest good.
Existing in the midst of ignorance, yet considering themselves wise and learned, these deluded ones wander about, stumbling like blind men led by one who is himself blind. (KaU 2.5)

But those people who partake in saṃsāra, dwelling in the midst of ignorance as if in dense darkness, being entangled by hundreds of snares of craving for children, cattle, and so forth— even though they consider themselves wise, intelligent, learned, and skilled in the scriptures—
they wander about excessively, following crooked and manifold paths, and are encompassed by the sufferings of old age, death, disease, and the like.

Just as many blind people, led by one who is himself blind and devoid of sight, encounter great misfortune on a treacherous path, so it is with those who are deluded and lacking in discrimination. KaUBh_2.5/1, 2.5.

The world beyond does not reveal itself to the fool who is heedless, deluded by the infatuation for wealth, and who thinks, "This world exists, but there is no other"; such a one, imagining thus, falls again and again under my sway. (KaU 2.6)

For this very reason, due to his state of delusion, the *sāmparāya* does not appear to him. *Sāmparāya* is that which pertains to the transition (*sampareyate*); it refers to the other world (*paraloka*), and specifically to the particular scriptural means for the purpose of attaining it. That *sāmparāya* does not appear—that is, it does not manifest or present itself—to the fool, the one lacking discrimination.

To one who is negligent—performing acts of heedlessness with a mind attached to the interests of sons, cattle, and so forth; likewise, one who is deluded by the infatuation for wealth, that is, by a lack of discrimination caused by wealth, and is shrouded in darkness (tamas)—to such a person, this very world which is visible, distinguished by women, food, drink, and the like, exists, but there is no other unseen world. Thus thinking, the conceited one (mānī) repeatedly takes birth and falls under my power, that is, into subjection to me, Death.
The meaning is that one remains mounted upon the very stream of suffering characterized by birth, death, and so forth;
for, as a general rule, the world is indeed of such a nature.

He who is not obtained even for hearing by many, and whom many, though hearing, do not perceive—wonderful is the speaker who has mastered him; wonderful is the one who understands him, being well-instructed by the skillful teacher. (KaU 2.7)

But among thousands who seek the highest good, perhaps only one in a thousand becomes a knower of the Self like you; for this Self is not to be obtained even by hearing—that is, even for the purpose of hearing, it is not found by many. Although many others hear, they do not know this Self; those who are unfortunate and whose minds are unpurified do not perceive it.
Moreover, even regarding this [knowledge], its speaker is someone rare and truly wonderful among many;

likewise, even after hearing it, one who has mastered it for oneself is someone truly skilled and proficient among many. For only a rare knower is "instructed by the skilled"—that is, instructed by a skillful and proficient teacher (*ācārya*; the word *saṃśikṣitaḥ*, "thoroughly trained," is to be supplied). KaU Bh 2.7.1–2.7.2.
This [Self] is not easily understood when taught by an inferior person, for it is conceived in many ways;
there is no path here when taught by another, for it is subtler than the subtlest, being beyond the reach of logic and smaller than an atom.

Why? Because this Self about which you ask me has not been well or correctly explained by an inferior person—that is, by one who is lowly or of limited intellect. It cannot be easily understood because it is conceived in many ways by disputants—as existing or non-existing, as the agent or the non-agent, as pure or impure, and so forth in numerous ways.

How, then, can it be well understood? It is said: when taught by one who is not other—that is, by a teacher who perceives no difference and has become one with the Brahman-Self that is to be realized.
The "course" (*gati*) has been described as manifold regarding the Self, characterized by such notions as "it exists" or "it does not exist. Here, however, in this Self, there is no such course;
it does not exist, because all courses of conceptual construction have subsided in the Self.

Alternatively, when the Self is described as being one's own self—non-different from oneself—then in that description of non-difference, there is no course consisting of the perception of another, because there is no other object of knowledge (*jñeya*) apart from it.
For this is the supreme culmination of knowledge: the realization of the oneness of the Self.
Therefore, because there is nothing further to be understood, no further progress remains here;
nor is there any movement within cyclic existence (saṃsāra) once the non-dual Self has been taught, since liberation—the fruit of that realization—is inseparable from it.
Alternatively, when the Self is taught by a teacher who has become one with Brahman, there is no failure to reach it, no lack of understanding, and no non-comprehension regarding that Self;
rather, the listener certainly attains realization concerning it, thinking "I am non-different from that," just as the teacher does.
Thus, the Self is easily understood when taught by a teacher who has realized the scriptures as being non-different from himself.

Otherwise, the Self would become even smaller than the minute, smaller even than the measure of an atom; for it is inconceivable and beyond reasoning, to be known only through one's own direct intuition and not by mere logic. For when someone has established the Self as having the dimension of an atom, another might then infer it to be even smaller than that.
"Even beyond that, there is something subtler still;
thus, indeed, there is no finality for reasoning anywhere. (KaU 2.8)
This wisdom cannot be attained by mere reasoning; it must be taught by another who has realized it for the sake of right knowledge, O dearest one.
You have indeed attained it, for you are firm in truth; may we have another son like you, O dear Naciketas!

Therefore, this understanding of the Self—which arises from what has been taught by another and is established by scripture—is not to be removed by reasoning, that is, by mere intellectual speculation; nor is it to be attained [by such means]. Alternatively, "not to be removed" means it is not to be abandoned.
For the dialectician, being ignorant of scripture, speculates on whatever he pleases, constructed solely by his own intellect.

And for this very reason, O dearest one (*preṣṭha*), that wisdom which is derived from scripture becomes easy to understand only when it is taught by a teacher who is himself conversant with scripture and distinct from a mere logician. What, then, is this wisdom inaccessible to reasoning? It is that wisdom which you have attained through the granting of my boon.

"O Naciketas, you are indeed one whose steadfastness (dhṛti) is true and whose object is not false; thus, O Satyadhṛti! Alas!"—with these words, Death spoke out of compassion in order to praise the knowledge that was about to be imparted.
"May there be another like you—a peerless questioner—to us, whether as a son or a disciple; may such a one arise."
Of what sort? Of the same sort as you, O Naciketas, the questioner. (KaU 2.9)
"I know that which is called a treasure is impermanent; for by means of unstable things, that which is stable cannot be attained.
Therefore, the Nāciketa fire-altar has been built by me; through unstable materials, I have attained the eternal. (KaU 2.10)
Being pleased once more, he said: "I know that the treasure (*śevadhi*), which is a storehouse characterized by the fruits of karma, is sought after like a treasure.
I know that this [treasure] is impermanent and not eternal.
For indeed, by means of things that are impermanent and unstable, that which is permanent and stable—the treasure called the Supreme Self—is not attained."
However, that treasure which consists of impermanent pleasure is indeed obtained through impermanent substances;

therefore, even though I knew this, thinking "the eternal is obtained through impermanent means," the fire-altar named Nāciketa was built— meaning that the fire which serves as the means for attaining heavenly bliss was brought into being by means of impermanent substances such as animals and the like.
Therefore, having attained that qualification, I have reached the eternal realm of Yama known as heaven, which is eternal yet relative.

Having seen the attainment of desires, the foundation of the world, the infinity of ritual action, and the further shore of fearlessness— the great, far-reaching praise that is the ultimate support— you, O wise Naciketas, have renounced them through steadfastness.
But you [attain] the attainment and fulfillment of desire— for here indeed all desires are completely fulfilled—
and the foundation and support of the world, consisting of the self, the elements, and the divine, because [He] is the Self of all.
The fruit of the meditation on *kratu* (volition) is the station of Hiraṇyagarbha, which is infinite;
and the further shore of fearlessness, which is the ultimate culmination.
It is the praiseworthy Great One, a collection of many qualities such as the supernatural powers (*aṇimā*) and so forth.
Having seen even that unsurpassed foundation— the greatness of the hymn (stomamahat) because it is beyond all comparison,
and the wide-reaching path (urugāya)— Naciketas,
being wise and steadfast through fortitude, has utterly cast them aside; desiring only the Supreme, you have renounced everything.

Having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self that God is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret cave, situated in the abyss, and ancient, the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow. (KaU 2.12)

That Self which you desire to know is difficult to perceive—meaning its perception is achieved with difficulty—because of its extreme subtlety; it is hidden and profound, concealed from the cognitions of ordinary objects and their modifications. It is "placed in the cave," meaning it resides in the intellect (*buddhi*), because it is perceived therein.
"Abiding in the abyss" (*gahvareṣṭhaṃ*) means that he dwells in the abyss—that is, in the unevenness of manifold calamities and perils.

Because he has thus entered into what is hidden and is seated in the cave of the heart, he is "abiding in the abyss" and consequently difficult to perceive. That ancient one, the primordial, having withdrawn the mind from sense objects through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self (*adhyātmayoga*), [one perceives him] within the self.
Concentration is internal yoga; through the attainment of that, the wise man, having realized the Self as God, abandons joy and sorrow arising from the absence of increase and decrease in himself.

Having heard this and having fully grasped it, a mortal who has extracted this subtle, righteous principle and attained it rejoices, for he has found that which is worthy of joy; I consider the abode to be opened for Naciketas.

Moreover, having heard this true nature of the Self which I shall declare, and having correctly grasped and taken it up through the grace of the Teacher, a mortal— one subject to death— having extracted and set aside from dharma that which is contrary to dharma, and having separated this subtle, atomic Self from the body and other such things, that wise mortal, having attained it, rejoices in that which is worthy of joy.

Having attained a self worthy of joy, I consider this very abode of Brahman—this mansion—to have its doors opened for you, Naciketas; that is to say, its gates are unveiled, wide open, and turned toward you; the intention is that I consider you worthy of liberation.
Apart from dharma and apart from adharma, apart from what has been done and what has not been done,
apart from what has been and what is to be— tell me that which you perceive.
Having heard this, Naciketas spoke again: "If I am worthy and if you, O Blessed One, are gracious toward me,
[then tell me that which] is distinct from dharma— meaning from scriptural duty, from its fruit, and from its performers."
Likewise, apart from unrighteousness— which consists of the non-performance of what is prescribed— and likewise apart from this [world] consisting of the performed and the unperformed;
"performed" refers to the effect and "unperformed" refers to the cause, and it is apart from these.

Furthermore, tell me of that reality which you perceive and know to be beyond the past that has ceased, the future that is yet to be, and likewise the present; the meaning is that it is not delimited by the three periods of time—that such a thing, which transcends the sphere of all worldly transactions, you behold and understand. KaUBh 2.14.1, 2.14.2.
That goal which all the Vedas proclaim, and which all austerities declare, desiring which they lead the life of a student—that goal I tell you briefly: it is "Om."

To him who had thus questioned, Death spoke, desiring to state both the subject asked about and further qualifications: "That goal which all the Vedas declare as that which is to be reached and attained without distinction or contradiction;
and all austerities (*tapas*) speak of it, meaning they have it as their purpose for attainment;
and desiring which, people practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*), characterized by dwelling in the teacher's house, or other [means] for the sake of attaining Brahman."

That state which you desire to know, I shall tell you to you in brief, in summary: it is "Om. This very state which you wish to understand is that which is expressed by the word "Om" and has the word "Om" as its symbol.
For this very syllable is Brahman; for this very syllable is the Supreme.
Having known this very syllable, whatever one desires becomes his.
Therefore, this very syllable is indeed the lower Brahman, and this very syllable is also the higher;
for this syllable is the symbol (pratīka) of those two.
Having known and meditated upon this very syllable as Brahman—
Whatever one desires, whether it be the higher or the lower, that becomes his:
if it is the higher, it is to be known; if it is the lower, it is to be attained.
This is the most excellent object of focus; this is the supreme object of focus.
Having known this object of focus, one is glorified in the world of Brahman. (KaU 2.17)
Precisely because it is so, this object of focus is the best and most praiseworthy among all objects for attaining Brahman.
This object of focus is both supreme and non-supreme, because its domain is both the supreme and the non-supreme Brahman.
Having known this object of focus, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.
The meaning is that, having become Brahman, one becomes worthy of worship like Brahman, both in the higher Brahman and in the lower Brahman.

By the passage beginning with "other than dharma" (KaU 2.14), the syllable *oṃ* is indicated as both the object of focus and the meditative symbol (*pratīka*) for the Self that was questioned— which is devoid of all particular attributes—
and likewise for the lower Brahman, for the sake of those practitioners who are dull-witted or of middling capacity.
Now, in order to determine directly the true nature of that Self which has the syllable *Oṃ* as its object of meditation, this is said:
"The wise one is neither born nor does he die; this one has not come from anywhere, nor has anything become him.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, he is not slain when the body is slain. (KaU 2.18)

It is not born, it does not arise, nor does it die; for an impermanent entity subject to origination, there are many modifications, the first and last of which are characterized by birth and destruction.
Here, these two modifications are negated with respect to the Self—first, with the phrase "it is not born, nor does it die"—for the purpose of negating all modifications.
He is all-seeing and wise,
because his nature is consciousness that is never lost;
moreover, this Self did not arise from any other cause, nor was it produced.
And because there is nothing whatsoever that exists as a distinct entity (arthāntara) from this self,
therefore this self is unborn, eternal, constant, and free from decay;
for whatever is non-eternal undergoes decay.
But this [Self] is eternal, and for that very reason ancient; it is "ancient" (purāṇa) because even in the past it was ever-new.

For that which is produced by means of the accumulation of parts is new at present, such as a sprout and so forth; however, the Self is the opposite of that—it is ancient, meaning it is devoid of growth.
Since this is so, it is not killed, nor is it harmed, even when the body is being struck by weapons and the like.
Even though situated therein, it is just like space.
If the slayer thinks to slay, or if the slain thinks himself slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. (KaU 2.19)
Even though the Self is thus [eternal], if one who perceives the body alone as the Self thinks— “I am the killer,” “I shall kill him”—
and if the other who is killed also thinks that he has killed himself, “I have been killed,” then both of them fail to know their own Self.

Since this Self does not kill because it is changeless, and likewise is not killed because it is changeless like space, therefore transmigration—characterized by merit, demerit, and so forth—belongs only to one who does not know the Self; for one who knows the Self, merit, demerit, and the rest are untenable, both on the authority of scripture and through logical reasoning.
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being.
Devoid of desire, one beholds Him—the majesty of the Self—through the clarity of the elements, and is freed from sorrow. (KaU 2.20)
But how is it said that the Self knows itself? It is subtler than the subtle, being more minute than the *śyāmāka* grain and other such things;
it is greater than the great, being larger than the vast dimensions of the earth and other such things.
Whatever object exists in the world, whether minute or great, it comes to possess a self by means of that very eternal Self.
When that [Self] is separated from the self, it becomes non-existent.
Therefore, this very Self is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, because it possesses all names, forms, and objects as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
And that Self is situated as the very essence of this living being—the entire class of creatures from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—hidden in the cave of the heart; this is the meaning.

The meaning is that when one perceives that Self—which is characterized by seeing, hearing, thinking, and cognizing; which is devoid of volitional action and desire; and whose intellect has ceased from external objects whether seen or unseen—then the organs such as the mind and the *dhātus* (elements), because they sustain the body, become serene. Through the serenity of these *dhātus*, one realizes the greatness of the Self, which is free from increase or decrease caused by karma.
He sees, "I am this," and knows it directly;
thereupon he becomes free from sorrow. (KaU Bh 2.20)
Otherwise, this Self is difficult for those who desire sense-objects and for ordinary people to understand, because:
"Seated, he goes far; lying down, he goes everywhere.
Who other than me is able to know that God, who is both intoxication and non-intoxication? (KaU 2.21)
Sitting, he remains truly unmoving; while lying down, he travels far; while sleeping, he goes everywhere.

Thus this divine Self is both intoxicated and non-intoxicated, both joyful and joyless, possessing contradictory attributes. Therefore, because it is impossible to know Him—who is the divine one beyond intoxication—who else but Me is capable of knowing that divine being?

This Self is to be known only by a learned person of subtle intellect such as ourselves; because it possesses various contradictory attributes—such as staying and moving, or being eternal and non-eternal—it is possessed of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmavān*). Like the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), it appears to someone like the universal form (*viśvarūpa*). Therefore, he demonstrates its difficulty of comprehension by saying, "Who other than me is capable of knowing it?"
The "lying down" (śayana) is the cessation of the instruments (karaṇa); it is the cessation of the partial cognition produced by the instruments that occurs for one who is lying down.

And when, because it consists solely of general cognition, it seems to go everywhere, then—while remaining established in its own nature and situated in specific cognitions—it seems to travel far during the movements of the mind and other organs due to those limiting adjuncts (upādhi), even though it remains right here.
Having realized the Self—bodiless within bodies that are unstable, great, and all-pervading—the wise man does not grieve. (KaU 2.22)
And he also shows that through the knowledge of that [Self], there is the transcendence of sorrow: "The bodiless Self, which by its own nature is like space—
[the text says] that bodiless one who abides within bodies, i.e., within the unstable and harmful impermanent bodies of gods, ancestors, humans, and so forth, is eternal and unchanging."
Regarding the doubt that "greatness" might imply a state of indifference, he says [the Self is] "vibhu," meaning all-pervading.
The use of the word "ātman" is for the purpose of demonstrating its non-difference from itself.
The word "ātman" is primarily applied to the inner self (pratyagātman); having realized such a Self as "I am this," [one attains liberation].
The steadfast and wise man does not grieve;
for such a knower of the Self, the arising of grief is simply impossible.
This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing.
Only by the one whom this Self chooses is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form. (KaU 2.23)

Although this Self is difficult to know, it is nevertheless easily known through the proper means; thus he says: this Self is not to be obtained—that is, known—by sacred teaching, meaning by the mastery of many Vedas, nor by intelligence, meaning by the power of retaining the meaning of texts, nor by mere extensive learning alone.
By what means, then, is [the Self] obtained? It is said: by that very Self which this practitioner chooses—that is, prays for—it is by that choosing Self itself that the Self is obtained and known.
And one who is free from desire prays for the Self alone;
the meaning is that the Self is obtained by the Self alone.
How is this obtained? It is said: for one who desires the Self, this Self reveals—that is, makes manifest—its own ultimate body; the meaning is its own true nature.
"One who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor is tranquil, nor is composed, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, shall not attain Him by means of wisdom. (KaU 2.24)
Furthermore: he is not one who has refrained from or desisted from misconduct—that is, from sinful actions prohibited by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*;
nor is he one who is unpeaceful or undisciplined due to the restlessness of the senses;
nor is he one who is unconcentrated, lacking one-pointedness of mind, and having a distracted consciousness.
Even while possessing a concentrated mind, because he desires the fruit of concentration, his mind is neither unpeaceful nor distracted;
through wisdom—that is, through the knowledge of Brahman—he may attain this very Self under discussion.
But he who has desisted from misconduct and from the restlessness of the senses, [attains it].

The meaning is that one whose mind is concentrated, whose mind is pacified even through the fruit of concentration, and who has a teacher, attains the Self as described by means of wisdom. // KaUBh 2.24.1, 2.24 //
He for whom both the priesthood and the nobility are the rice, and for whom death is the sauce—who truly knows where he is? KaU 2.25.1, 2.25.2.
Thus ends the second Vallī in the Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad. // 2 //
But he who is not thus— that Self for whom both Brahman and Kṣatra (the priestly and warrior orders), though they uphold all laws, become food to be consumed by him everywhere;
and even Death, the destroyer of all, becomes like a condiment to his rice,
being insufficient even as food— [that is the Self].

Who, being of ordinary intellect and lacking the aforementioned means, would know (*veda*) him—that is, perceive him as "this very one," meaning as one possessing the aforementioned means—wherein that Self resides? Thus ends KaU 2.25.1–2.25.2.
Thus ends the commentary on the second Vallī of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.

Now begins the third chapter (Vallī). Drinking the fruit of their good deeds in the world, having entered the cave in the highest upper realm, those who know Brahman call them "Shadow and Light," as do those who maintain the five fires and those who have thrice performed the Nāciketa rite. (KaU 3.1)
The connection of this section beginning with "Two drinking the Truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*) is as follows:
although knowledge and ignorance have been introduced as distinct and having contrary fruits, they have not yet been precisely determined along with their respective results.
The metaphor of the chariot is devised for the purpose of determining that [distinction], and thus there is ease of comprehension.

In this way, by means of the metaphor of the chariot intended to distinguish between the attainer and the attainable, or the goer and the goal, two selves are presented: "drinking" (pibantau) the fruit of action, which is "ṛta" and "satya" because it is inevitable.

In that state, one [of the two] alone drinks and enjoys the fruit of karma, yet the other is also said to "drink" due to its connection with the drinker, according to the maxim of the umbrella-bearer (*cchatrinyāya*).
The word *ṛtam* (the fruit) refers to the well-performed action done by oneself; this is to be connected with what precedes.
"In this world" means within this body.
They have entered the cave within the cave of the intellect.
It is "supreme" (paramam) in comparison to the external space occupied by the cosmic Person.
It is the "half of the beyond" (parārdhe); the half of the supreme Brahman, its location, is the "half of the beyond," namely the space within the heart (hārdākāśam).
For in that [space] the Supreme Brahman is perceived;
therefore, the meaning is that they have entered that supreme, highest goal, the space within the heart (*hārdākāśa*).
And those who know Brahman speak of them as being distinct from one another, like shadow and light, by virtue of their states as the transmigrating soul and the non-transmigrating Self.
Not only do those who perform no ritual acts say this,
but so too do the householders who maintain the five fires and those who have performed the Triṇāciketa sacrifice.
Those by whom the Nāciketa fire has been built three times are the "Triṇāciketas. (KaU 1.1) / (KaUBh 3.1) / (KaUBh 3.1)
May we be able to attain the Nāciketa fire— that bridge for those who have sacrificed, that which is the imperishable, supreme Brahman, the fearless further shore for those desiring to cross over.

That which is a bridge— like a bridge, a bridge— for those who have sacrificed, for those performing sacrifices, and for those engaged in ritual action, because it serves the purpose of crossing over suffering;
that Nāciketa fire, may we be able to know and to comprehend it.

Furthermore, may we be able to know that which is fearless and free from fear— the imperishable Brahman called the Self, which is the supreme refuge for those who know Brahman and who desire to cross over, wishing to reach the further shore of saṃsāra.
The meaning of the sentence is that both the higher and the lower Brahman, which serve as the refuge for those engaged in ritual action and those who know Brahman respectively, are to be known.
For it is precisely these two that were introduced by the statement, "The two drinking the reward" (KaU 3.1).
Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot;
know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind indeed as the reins. (KaU 3.3)

In this context, for that transmigrating being who is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is subject to both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*— the former for proceeding toward liberation and the latter for proceeding through transmigratory existence)—
for him, a chariot is conceived as the means for those two modes of travel.
In this regard, know and understand the Self (*ātman*), the transmigrator, to be the rider, the owner of the chariot.

The body is indeed the chariot, because the body is drawn along by the senses which occupy the place of horses harnessed to a chariot. Know the intellect, characterized by determination, to be the charioteer; for the body is primarily guided by the intellect, just as a chariot is primarily guided by a charioteer.
For almost all activity pertaining to the body must indeed be performed by the intellect.
Know the mind—characterized by volition, doubt, and so forth—to be the rein or bridle;
for the senses, such as hearing and the rest, proceed only when restrained by the mind, just as horses are controlled by a bridle. (KaU 3.3–4)
The wise say that the senses are the horses and the objects are their paths;
they say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. (KaU 3.4)

Those skilled in the construction of chariots call the sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, "horses," because they share the common quality of drawing [the body] along. Know that within those very sense faculties, which have been conceptualized as horses, the objects of perception— forms and so forth— are the paths.
The wise, those possessed of discernment, declare that the Self—joined with the body, senses, and mind, meaning associated with the body, senses, and mind—is the "experiencer" and the "transmigrator.
For the isolated Self has no status as an experiencer;
its experience-ship is produced solely by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi).
And so another scriptural passage shows that the pure [Self] is indeed a non-experiencer: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (BĀU 4.4.7), and so forth.

This being the case, the realization of the station of Viṣṇu as one's own Self through the metaphor of the chariot to be described is logically possible, and not otherwise, because that would involve overstepping its own nature.
But for one who lacks discernment and whose mind is always undisciplined, the senses are uncontrollable, like the vicious horses of a charioteer. (KaU 3.5)

This being so, for one who lacks discernment—whose charioteer, called "intellect," is undiscerning, unskilled, and lacking discrimination regarding both engagement and withdrawal—the senses, which stand in the place of horses, become ungovernable and impossible to restrain; they are like the vicious, untamed horses of another charioteer who is always joined with a mind that stands in the place of reins, but which is unapplied, unrestrained, and unconcentrated upon the path of the chariot. (KaU 3.5)
But for one who possesses discernment and whose mind is always disciplined, the senses are under control, like well-trained horses are under a charioteer. (KaU 3.6)

But as for the charioteer who is the opposite of what was previously described—one who is wise, firm-minded, and always possessed of a concentrated mind—for him the senses, which correspond to the horses, can be directed forward or turned back; they are under his control, like well-trained, excellent horses, unlike those of the other charioteer.
But he who is devoid of knowledge, lacking a disciplined mind, and ever impure, does not attain that state; he enters into the cycle of rebirth.

He states the result of that aforementioned person who lacks discernment: "But he who is without discernment, who is mindless—that is, whose mind is not restrained—is for that very reason always impure.
He does not, by means of that driver, reach the previously mentioned Imperishable, which is the supreme state."
Not only does he not attain that [state], but he also undergoes saṃsāra, which is characterized by birth and death.
But he who possesses discernment, who is self-possessed and ever pure, attains that state from which he is not born again. (KaU 3.8)
But he who possesses discernment— like a charioteer endowed with discernment,
being wise and having his mind focused, possessed of the internal organ— he is therefore always pure;
he indeed attains that state.
Because, having not fallen away from that state attained through the authoritative teacher, one is not born again in saṃsāra.
But that man who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the journey— that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

What is that state? He says: he who has consciousness as his charioteer—that is, he who has the intellect of discrimination as his charioteer, as previously described—and who possesses the reins of the mind, whose mind is restrained, and whose heart is composed; such a pure and wise man reaches the very end of the path, which is the supreme goal to be attained, and is liberated from all the bonds of worldly existence.
That is the supreme, most excellent station (*pada*), which is the true reality (*satattva*) of Viṣṇu— the all-pervading Brahman, the Supreme Self known as Vāsudeva— which the wise man attains.

Now, this [section] is begun for the purpose of attaining that state which is to be reached by means of realizing the inner self through a sequence of gradations of subtlety, beginning with the gross sense organs:
"Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind;
higher than the mind is the intellect; higher than the intellect is the Great Self. (KaU 3.10)

The sense organs are, first of all, gross; those objects for which they were initiated to manifest themselves are subtler and greater than those sense organs—their respective effects—and are of the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Even beyond those objects is the mind, which is more subtle, greater, and of the nature of the inner self.
That which is denoted by the word "mind" (*manas*) is the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*) that constitutes the mind, because it initiates volition (*saṅkalpa*), doubt (*vikalpa*), and so forth.
Higher than even the mind is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is more subtle, greater, and of the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*);
that which is denoted by the word "intellect" is the subtle element that initiates determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth.

The Self is the "Uddhara" because it is the innermost self (*pratyagātman*) of the intellects of all living beings; it is the "Great Self" (*mahān ātmā*) because of its greatness compared to everything else. That principle which first arose from the Unmanifest—the Hiraṇyagarbha reality consisting of both consciousness and unconsciousness—is called the Great Self, and it is said to be beyond the intellect.
Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest; greater than the Unmanifest is the Person (Puruṣa). There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.
Even greater than the great, more subtle than the subtlest, the innermost self, and greater than all else is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
It is the seed of the entire world, whose name and form are undifferentiated (*avyākṛta-nāmarūpa*), the true essence (*satattva*) consisting of a convergence of all causal and efficient potencies.

This Unmanifest—which cannot be designated by names such as "unmanifest space" (*avyākṛtākāśa*) and so forth—is woven like warp and woof within the Supreme Self, as it were, within the seed of a banyan tree.
It is like the potentiality of the banyan tree.

Therefore, it is higher than the unmanifest (avyakta), more subtle because it is the cause of all causes, and great because it is the inner self (pratyagātman); for this very reason it is the Puruṣa, because it fills everything.
Then, warding off the objection that there might be something else beyond this, he says: "There is nothing whatsoever beyond the Puruṣa.

Since there is no other entity whatsoever superior to the Puruṣa, who is the dense mass of pure consciousness, therefore He is the ultimate limit, the finality, and the culmination of subtlety, greatness, and the nature of being the innermost Self.

For here, beginning from the senses, [the qualities] such as subtlety and so forth reach their culmination. And for this very reason, it is the supreme, most excellent goal for those transmigrating beings who possess the capacity to go everywhere. As it is said: "Having gone there, they do not return" (BhG 15.6).
Thus [it is stated] in the Smṛti. (KaU Bh 3.11)
This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
yet it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect. (KaU 3.12)
But if there is going, there must also be coming; how then can it be said, "from which one is not born again" (KaU 3.8)?
This is not a fault.
Because [the Self] is the innermost Self (pratyagātman) of everything, realization itself is figuratively called "going.
And that state of being the innermost Self has been demonstrated by its transcendence over the senses, mind, and intellect.
For whoever is a goer goes toward that which is not of the nature of the innermost Self—that is, he does not find his own true nature, which is non-self.
And thus says the Śruti: "Those who have no path [yet] reach the end of paths" (Itihāsa-Upaniṣad 18), and so forth.
Likewise, it demonstrates that the inner self (pratyagātman) is common to all:

this Puruṣa is hidden and concealed within all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; enveloped by the functions of seeing, hearing, and so on, and covered by ignorance and māyā, for this very reason the Self does not manifest as the Self.
To someone [else],
it may seem that this illusion is exceedingly profound, difficult to fathom, and manifold,
in that every living being— though in the ultimate sense identical with the ultimate reality— is not grasped as "I am the Supreme Self," even when being thus instructed.

One grasps as the Self the non-Self—the aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth—which, though appearing as the object of the Self, is like a jar or other external objects; even while not saying "I am the son of such-and-such," one accepts it as the Self.
Surely, being utterly deluded by the Māyā of the Supreme Being alone, the entire world wanders about.
And thus there is the Smṛti: "I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my Yogamāyā" (BhG 7.25), and so forth.
Is it not a contradiction to say both, "The wise man, having realized this, does not grieve" (KaU 2.22) and "it does not shine forth" (KaU 3.12)?
This is not so.
It was stated that because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not an object of cognition, it does not manifest; however,

it is seen by means of that supreme conditioned [wisdom], which is like the peak itself— by that which is "supreme" because it is endowed with one-pointedness, and "subtle" because it is intent upon the investigation of subtle reality.
By whom?

By those of subtle vision (*sūkṣmadarśibhiḥ*), that is, by the wise whose nature it is to perceive the ultimate subtlety through a succession of subtleties, according to the manner [of the teaching] beginning with "the objects are indeed beyond the senses. By those subtle-seers, the wise.
Thus [ends] this [section]. KaUBh 3.12.1, 3.12.3.
The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should restrain those two in the self of knowledge;
he should restrain that knowledge in the Great Self; and he should restrain that in the peaceful Self.

He states the means for attaining that: "The wise one, the discerning one, should restrain—that is, control and withdraw—what? Speech, which here serves as an illustration for all the sense organs. "Speech" refers to speech itself.
Where? In the mind (*manasi*). The lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasaṃ dairghyam*).
And one should restrain that mind in knowledge—that is, in the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the self (*ātman*) whose nature is luminosity.
For the intellect (buddhi) pervades the instruments such as the mind (manas) and so forth, and the Self is their inner witness.
One should restrain knowledge within the intellect, which is situated in the Great First-born Self.
The meaning is that one should bring about the Self’s consciousness to possess a nature as clear as that of the First-born itself.

And one should restrain that great Self within the primary Self—the Self which is peaceful, whose form is such that all distinctions have subsided, which is changeless, most internal, and the witness of all cognitions and mental states.
"Arise! Awake! Having reached the excellent [teachings], understand them!
The edge of a razor is sharp and difficult to traverse; the sages call that a path hard to travel."
