Thus, when a person has dissolved within the Self all three—name, form, and action—which are the manifestations of false knowledge and are characterized by action, agent, and fruit; and who, through the knowledge of the true nature of his own Self, becomes established in himself, tranquil, and fulfilled, just as one becomes so upon seeing the true nature of a mirage, a rope, or the sky, [and thus perceiving] the water of a mirage, a snake in a rope, or impurities in the sky as they truly are; for this reason:
Therefore, for the sake of seeing that [Reality], arise, O living beings, who have been sleeping since beginningless time!
Turn toward the knowledge of the Self and, remaining awake, bring about the destruction of the sleep of ignorance— which is of terrible form and the seed of all misfortune.
How?
Having approached and attended upon excellent, preeminent teachers who know reality,
understand— realize— that the Self, which is within all, as taught by them, is "I am."

For the Śruti, out of compassion like a mother, says that one must not remain indifferent, because the object of knowledge is within the domain of extremely subtle intellect. What, then, is this "subtle intellect"? It is explained as follows:
The edge of a razor is sharpened, keen, and difficult to traverse—that which is difficult to cross over is "duratyayā.
Just as that [edge] is difficult to tread upon with the feet, so too is this path difficult to accomplish; thus the wise, the intelligent ones, speak of that path characterized by knowledge.
The intention is that because the object of knowledge is extremely subtle, they say that the path of knowledge regarding it is difficult to accomplish.
How, then, is it said that the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is extremely subtle?
First, this earth is gross, being composed of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, and serving as the object of all the sense-faculties; the same is true of the body.

In that regard, by the gradual removal of each quality among smell and the others, a gradation of subtlety, magnitude, purity, permanence, and so forth is observed in water and the other elements, up to space (*ākāśa*).

All those [qualities] beginning with smell and ending with sound are merely modifications because they are gross; where these do not exist, what need is there to mention its subtlety and its state of being unsurpassed? The Śruti shows this: "Having perceived that which is without sound, without touch, without form, undecaying, likewise without taste, eternal, and without smell; which is without beginning, without end, beyond the Great (Mahat), and fixed—one is released from the jaws of death. (KaU 3.15)

That which has been described as Brahman is soundless, touchless, formless, tasteless, and odorless; for it transcends that which possesses sound and the other qualities, whereas this [Brahman], because it lacks sound and the rest, is imperishable— it does not perish—
and for that very reason, it is eternal.
For that which passes away is impermanent, but this does not pass away; therefore, it is eternal.
Furthermore, it is eternal because it is beginningless—that is, it has no beginning (ādi) in the form of a cause.
For whatever has a beginning is impermanent due to being an effect and dissolves into its cause, such as the earth and other elements.
But this [Self], because it is the cause of all things, is unproduced; because it is unproduced, it is eternal, and there is no cause in which it could dissolve.
Likewise, it is infinite (*ananta*); since no end (*anta*) exists for it, it is infinite.

Just as the impermanence of things such as the plantain tree is observed even through the production of effects like fruit, yet Brahman is not likewise characterized by having an end; therefore, it is eternal. Indeed, Brahman is greater than the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), which is called the intellect (buddhi), because it is distinct from it and consists of the nature of eternal consciousness; for Brahman is the witness of all, being the self of all beings.
For it has been said: "He who dwells in all beings" (KaU 3.12), and so forth.
And this is eternal, immovable, and absolute; it is not a relative eternity like that of the earth and other elements.

Having perceived—that is, having realized—Brahman as the Self which is of such a nature, one is liberated, is set free, from the jaws of death, from the domain of death characterized by ignorance, desire, and action. (KaUBh 3.15)
Having recited and having heard this eternal narrative of Naciketas as proclaimed by Death, the wise man is glorified in the world of Brahman. (KaU 3.16)

In order to praise the knowledge under discussion, the Śruti says: "Having studied this ancient (sanātana) narrative— the Nāciketa, so called because it was obtained by Naciketas, and the Mṛtyuproktam, so called because it was proclaimed by Death— characterized by three chapters (vallīs), having heard it from the Brāhmaṇas and from teachers, the wise man [attains] the Brahmaloka, which is Brahman itself as the world."
The meaning is that in that world of Brahman, he is honored; that is to say, he becomes the very Self, the one to be worshipped.
Whoever, being self-restrained, should proclaim this supreme secret in an assembly of Brahmins, or at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, that leads to infinity; it leads to infinity. KaU 3.17.1, 3.17.3.
Thus ends the third Vallī in the Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad.

Whoever, having become restrained and pure, should cause this supreme, most excellent, secret, and hidden text to be heard— both in its words and its meaning— in an assembly of Brahmins, that is, in an assembly of the Veda, or should cause it to be heard at the time of a *śrāddha* by those who are eating, that *śrāddha* of his conduces to and results in infinite fruit, leading to infinity.
The repetition is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. (KaUBh 3.17)
Thus ends the commentary on the third Vallī of the Kaṭhavallī.
Now begins the second chapter.

It has been stated: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by means of the highest intellect" (KaU 3.12). What, then, is the obstacle to the highest intellect, such that in its absence the Self is not seen? This subsequent section (*vallī*) is commenced for the purpose of demonstrating the cause of that non-perception.
For when the cause that obstructs the highest good is known, an effort can be undertaken to remove it, and not otherwise:
"The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self.
Some wise man, desiring immortality, looked within at the inward self with his eyes turned back. (KaU 4.1) (1.1)
"They go forth, they move away"— thus, the apertures, specifically the sense organs such as the ears and so forth, are called "apertures" (*khāni*).
These indeed function only directed outward (*parāñci*) for the purpose of manifesting objects such as sound and the like.
Because he thus destroyed—that is, pierced or killed—those things which possess intrinsic nature;
who was he? The Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), the Supreme Lord, who is always independent and not dependent on another.

Therefore, the perceiver sees and perceives external objects—sound and the rest—which are of an outward nature and not the self; he does not perceive the inner self, meaning that he does not perceive his own inner self.

Even though the world is of such a nature, a certain wise, intelligent, and discriminating person proceeds against the current of the river, as it were, toward the *pratyagātmā*—that which is both "inner" (*pratyak*) and the "self" (*ātman*).
In common usage, the word *ātman* is conventionally established only for the inner self and nowhere else.
Even according to the etymological view, the word *ātman* applies to that very [self]:
“Because it attains (*āpnoti*), because it takes up (*ādatte*), because it eats (*atti*) objects here,
and because its state is continuous (*santato bhāvaḥ*), it is therefore celebrated as the *ātman*” (LiP 1.70.96).
Thus, because of the traditional derivation of the word *ātman*;
he "beheld" (*aikṣat*)—meaning he saw—that inner self (*pratyagātmā*), his own essential nature (*sva-svabhāva*).
This is because, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is no restriction regarding tense.

How does he see? It is said: "one whose eyes are turned away" (*āvṛttacakṣuḥ*). He is one whose collection of senses, such as the eyes and ears, has been turned away (*āvṛtta*) or withdrawn from all external objects; he is thus called "one whose eyes are turned away. Being thus refined, he sees the inner self (*pratyagātman*). For it is not possible for a single person to be intent on perceiving external objects and to perceive the inner self simultaneously.

But for what purpose does the steadfast one, having thus brought about the cessation of the activity of his own nature through such great effort, perceive the inner Self? It is said: "Desiring immortality"—that is, the state of being subject to no death, the eternal nature of the Self. (KaUBh 4.1/2, 1.1)
Fools pursue outward desires; they go to the snare of widespread death.
But the wise, having realized immortality, do not seek the permanent among the impermanent here on earth.
Insofar as that innate perception of the external is indeed a non-perception of the Self, it is the cause of obstruction to the vision of the Self because it is contrary to it;
and that thirst for enjoyments—both seen and unseen—which is displayed by ignorance (avidyā) directed solely toward the external, these two, ignorance and thirst, obstruct the vision of the Self.
Thus, one whose vision of the Self is obstructed by ignorance and thirst [pursues] only external objects of desire, those things to be desired.
Fools of little wisdom follow after and pursue sense objects;

for that reason, they go toward and enter the snare of death—which is the aggregate of ignorance, desire, and action—that is spread out, extensive, and all-pervading; it is called a "snare" (pāśa) because by it one is bound, characterized as the conjunction of the body, senses, and so forth.
The meaning is that they undergo an incessant multitude of misfortunes, such as birth, death, old age, disease, and so forth.
Since this is so, therefore the wise—those who possess discrimination—having realized the eternal immortality characterized by abiding in the nature of the inner self;

for while the immortality of the body and such is impermanent, this [immortality] characterized by abiding in the nature of the inner self is eternal, according to the Vedic scripture: "He does not increase by action, nor does he become less" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23).
Having thus understood that immortality— which is of such a nature, unchanging, and immovable— and having determined it among all unstable and impermanent objects,
the Brāhmaṇas here in this transmigratory world, which abounds in misfortune, do not desire anything at all, because [such desires] are contrary to the realization of the inner Self.
The meaning is that they indeed rise above the longings for sons, wealth, and worlds.
By means of this very [consciousness], one perceives form, taste, smell, sounds, and tactile objects of sexual union; what remains here [to be known] beyond this?
This indeed is that. KaU 4.3.2, 1.3.
Since the knowers of Brahman (brahmajñas) desire nothing other than consciousness (vijñāna), how is its realization attained? It is explained as follows:

by means of that self whose nature is consciousness, one clearly knows—i.e., perceives—the forms, tastes, smells, sounds, and touches, as well as sexual acts and the pleasant perceptions caused by sexual acts; thus does everyone [know].
The world [objects].
But surely, the world does not have such a well-known conviction as "I, who am distinct from the body and so forth, cognize";
rather, every person in the world understands it as "I, who am the aggregate of the body and so forth, cognize."
But it is not so;

since the aggregate of the body and so forth is no different from sound and other objects in its essential nature, and is likewise no different in being an object of cognition, it is not logical for it to be the cognizer.

For if the aggregate of the body and so forth, while consisting of form and the rest, were to cognize those very forms and so forth, then external forms and the rest would also cognize one another and their own respective natures.
But this is not the case.

Therefore, the world cognizes the objects characterized by the body and so forth—such as visible form and the rest—by means of this very self whose nature is consciousness, which is indeed distinct from the body and its like;
just as, for example, it is said that "fire is that by which iron burns."
What remains in this world that is unknowable by the self? Nothing whatsoever remains.
Rather, everything is indeed knowable by the self.
That self for which nothing remains unknowable is omniscient.
This indeed is that.

What is that? It is the supreme state of Viṣṇu, different from dharma and the like, about which even the gods and others have doubted, and than which there is nothing higher; this very thing has been attained—this is the meaning.
The wise person does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self by which one perceives both the state of dreaming and the state of waking.

Thinking that this matter is difficult to understand because of its extreme subtlety, he states this very point again and again: "the end of dream, the middle of dream, and that which is to be known in dream"; likewise, "the end of waking, the middle of waking, and that which is to be known in waking.
"The world perceives both the ends of dream and waking by means of that Self"—all of this is as explained previously.
Having realized and understood that great, all-pervading Self as one's own self—thinking directly, "I am the Supreme Self"—the wise man does not grieve.
He who knows this Self, the eater of honey, the living one in its proximity,
the lord of what has been and what is to be— he does not shrink away from it.
This indeed is that. KaU 4.5.2, 1.5.

Furthermore, whoever knows— directly, in close proximity— this Self (ātman), the consumer of honey, the enjoyer of the fruits of karma, the sustainer of the collection of vital functions beginning with breath, as the Ruler (īśāna) of the past and the future—
that is, of the three periods of time; thereafter, by virtue of that realization, he does not shrink from the Self, nor does he wish to hide it, because he has attained fearlessness.
For as long as one who stands in the midst of fear considers the self to be impermanent, so long does he desire to protect himself.
But when he realizes the self to be eternal and non-dual, then who would desire to protect what, or from what?
"This indeed is that," as before. (KaU 4.5) / 2,1.5 /
He who was born before the heat [of creation], who was born before the waters,
and who, having entered the cave, beheld him standing there together with all beings.
This indeed is that.

This shows that he who is designated as the inner self (pratyagātman) and the Lord (īśvara) is the Self of all: "Whosoever seeker of liberation [meditates] upon him who was born first—prior to the *tapas* characterized by knowledge and so forth, namely Hiraṇyagarbha—who is prior to what? He says: prior to the waters; the intention is that he is prior to the five elements joined with water, not to the waters alone."

He who perceived— that is, who sees— that one who was born, who arose, as the first-born, having produced the bodies of the gods and others, entered and dwells within the cave of all living beings, namely the space of the heart, experiencing sound and the other objects of sense, and remaining together with the elements characterized as the body and its organs.
He who sees thus sees that very thing which is the Brahman under discussion.
She who comes into being through the vital breath, Aditi, composed of the deities, who, having entered the secret cave, abides there and was born from all beings.
This indeed is that.

Furthermore—she who consists of all the gods, whose essence is all the gods, who arises from the supreme Brahman through the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, and who is Aditi because she devours (eats) sound and the other sense objects; her, as Aditi, who stands having entered the cave as before—that very one he further specifies: she who was born, that is, produced, Jātavedas has been deposited in the two kindling woods, well-nourished like an embryo by pregnant women; day after day Agni is to be praised by watchful men who bring oblations.
This indeed is that.
Furthermore— He who is the sacrificial fire (adhiyajña), established and situated within the upper and lower kindling woods (araṇī) as Jātavedas Agni, and who is again the consumer of all oblations;

and who, with respect to the self (adhyātma), is like the embryo within pregnant women by yogis, being well-nourished and properly sustained just as an embryo in the world is well-maintained through the consumption of blameless food and other such means.
Thus, he is well-praised by the officiating priests and the yogis.

Furthermore, day after day, he is to be honored, praised, and saluted by those engaged in ritual action and by the yogis, who remain wakeful—meaning vigilant and undistracted—in the sacrificial rite and in the heart respectively;
that is, by those possessing oblations such as clarified butter and by those possessing meditative contemplation and cultivation.
"By men, by humans"—Agni is indeed this very same primordial Brahman under discussion.
From whence the sun rises and whither it goes to set—therein all the gods are established; no one transcends that.
This indeed is that.
Moreover— since from that Prāṇa the sun rises, and into that very Prāṇa it goes to its setting day after day;

into that Prāṇa as the Self, all the gods— namely, Agni and the others with respect to the divine (adhidaiva), and speech and the others with respect to the individual self (adhyātma)— are all fixed and inserted like the spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel at the time of maintenance.
That too is indeed Brahman. This Brahman is the self of all. No one whatsoever, no one at all, transcends it; having transcended it, one does not go to a state of being other than its own nature.
This indeed is that. KaU Bh 4.9/2,1.9.
What is here is there; what is there is likewise here.
He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity.

Lest anyone should harbor the suspicion that the Self— which exists within all beings from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects— appears as a transmigrating being due to its association with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and is thus something other than the Supreme Brahman, the author says this: "That very same [Self] which here, associated with the adjuncts of cause and effect,

appears as possessing the attributes of transmigratory existence to those lacking discrimination, is itself situated in its own nature there [in liberation], having the essential character of eternal, dense consciousness."
Brahman is devoid of all the phenomena of saṃsāra.

That which abides there, in that other Self, is indeed this very same [reality] here, appearing differentiated through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name, form, effects, and instruments; it is nothing else.

This being so, one who is deluded by ignorance—characterized by the perception of difference in the nature of the adjuncts—regards this Brahman, which is non-dual, as "I am other than the Supreme," or "the Supreme Brahman is other than me."
He sees and perceives [the world] as if it were manifold and divided;
he goes from death to death—that is, he repeatedly undergoes the state of birth and death.
Therefore, one should not see it in that way.
The meaning of the sentence is that one should perceive: "I am indeed Brahman, which is of the single essence of consciousness, continuous, and all-pervading like space."
This must be attained by the mind alone; there is no diversity whatsoever here.
He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.11)

Prior to the realization of oneness, this Brahman—which is of a single flavor—must be attained by the mind alone, purified by the teacher’s traditional instruction, [realizing] "This is the Self itself; there is nothing else.
And once it is attained, because ignorance, which presents the appearance of manifoldness, has ceased, there is not even an atom of multiplicity here in this Brahman.
However, he who does not relinquish the vision blurred by the cataract of ignorance perceives, as it were, multiplicity within this Brahman.
The meaning is that he goes from death to death indeed, even by superimposing a slight distinction.
Furthermore, he speaks again of that very same primordial Brahman:
"The Person, the size of a thumb, stands in the midst of the self;
as the ruler of what has been and what is to be, one does not shrink away from him."
This indeed is that.

"Of the size of a thumb" means having the measurement of a thumb; the lotus of the heart is of that measurement, and [the self] exists within its cavity. Having the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it is "thumb-sized," like the space within a bamboo joint of thumb-size. It is a "Person" (*puruṣa*) because everything is filled by it.
Having known that Self, the Ruler of the past and the future, who dwells in the middle, within the body—that Self—[the result is as stated] previously, beginning with "not this," and so forth.
The Person, the size of a thumb, like a smokeless flame, is the Lord of what has been and what is to be; he is indeed today, and he is tomorrow.
This indeed is that.
Furthermore, the person the size of a thumb is like a smokeless light;
the term "smokeless" is appropriate because it refers to light.

He who is thus characterized by yogis as the Lord within the heart, the ruler of the past and the future—he alone is eternal and immutable. He who exists among living beings today will exist tomorrow as well.
The meaning is that no other like him shall be born, nor any other different from him.

By this, the position expressed in the verse, "Nor is there one who says, 'This does not exist'" (KaU 1.20), which—though not established by reasoning—is refuted by the scripture's own words; likewise, the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) is also refuted.
Just as water rained upon a mountain peak flows away in different directions,
so too one who perceives phenomena as separate runs after them alone.

Furthermore, he speaks of the denial of the perception of difference regarding Brahman: "Just as water rained upon and poured out on a difficult, inaccessible, elevated place flows away among the mountains—those possessing ridges—and into low-lying regions, becoming dispersed and perishing;
even so, one who perceives the attributes as distinct from the Self, seeing them separately in each body, follows after those very attributes which conform to the differences of the bodies."
The meaning is that he undergoes the dissolution of the body again and again, each time separately.
Just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it,
so does the self of the sage who understands become, O Gautama.
Thus ends the fourth Vallī in the Kaṭhaka Upaniṣad.

Furthermore, regarding this wise sage—one who has destroyed the perception of difference created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and perceives the Self as non-dual, a single essence of pure consciousness—how does his own true nature come to be?
It is said: just as water poured into or cast into pure, clear water becomes of one and the same taste.
It does not become otherwise; rather, it remains exactly as it is. In this very same way, O Gautama, the Self becomes one for the sage who is reflective and understands oneness.

Therefore, having abandoned the divisive view of false logicians and the evil views of nihilists, the vision of the oneness of the Self—taught by the Veda which desires our welfare even more than thousands of mothers and fathers—should be respectfully accepted by those whose pride has been stilled. This is the meaning.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth Vallī of the Kaṭhavallī.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
This undertaking is once again for the purpose of determining the true nature of Brahman through another method, because Brahman is difficult to comprehend:
"The city with eleven gates belongs to the Unborn One of unswerving mind."
Having performed [it], one does not grieve; being liberated, one is further released.
This indeed is that. KaU 5.1/2, 2.1.

The body is a city, like a city; for it is seen to possess the full array of various city-appurtenances, such as gatekeepers, superintendents, and so forth. Furthermore, a city together with its appurtenances is observed to exist for the sake of a sovereign who is himself uncomposed and independent.
Likewise, this body, being a collection of many instruments due to its similarity to a city, must exist for the sake of a master who is not himself a composite, standing in the place of a king.
And this city called the body has eleven gates; it has eleven gates: seven in the head, and three directed downward along with the navel.
There is one [door] in the head;
by these, there is a city with eleven gates.
Of what? Of the Unborn (aja), who is devoid of transformations such as birth and the like, the Self (ātman) who stands in the position of a king and is distinct from the characteristics of a city.

"Avakra-cetas" refers to one whose consciousness—meaning the mind—is straight (avakra), not crooked (akuṭila), like the light of the sun, eternally abiding, and uniform in nature; [the term denotes] that Brahman who is the sovereign (rājasthānīya) and possesses such a mind. Having approached—that is, having meditated upon—that Supreme Lord, the master of the city, of whom this city is the abode.
For meditation is its practice preceded by right knowledge.
Being liberated from all cravings, one who has meditated upon that [Self] as dwelling equally in all beings does not grieve.
Since fearlessness is attained through that knowledge, there is no occasion for sorrow; how, then, could there be any expectation of fear?
Right here he becomes liberated from the bonds of ignorance, desire, and karma;
and being liberated, he is released—meaning that he does not take up a body again.
The Swan dwelling in the pure, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling on the altar, the guest dwelling in the house, the dweller among men,
the dweller in the best, the dweller in Truth, the dweller in the sky, born of the waters, born of the cows, born of Truth, born of the mountains— the Great Truth.
But that Self does not reside only in one body or one city; rather, it resides in all cities.
How so? It is called *haṃsa* because it "goes" (*hanti*) or "moves. It is called *śuciṣat* because it "sits" (*sīdati*) in the pure [heaven] as the divine solar self.
He causes all to dwell, thus he is *vasu*.
He sits in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) in the form of the wind, thus he is *antarikṣasat*.
Agni is the *hotṛ*, according to the Vedic revelation: "Agni, indeed, is the *hotṛ*."

He is called *vediṣad* because he sits upon the altar (*vedi*), which is the earth, as indicated by the wording of the mantra beginning with, "This altar is the furthest limit of the earth" (Ṛgveda 2.3.20).
Being Soma, he is the guest (*atithi*) who sits in the dwelling (*duroṇa*), that is, in the jar; thus he is *duroṇasat*.
He sits in dwellings—that is, in houses—in the form of a Brahmin guest; he sits among men—that is, among human beings; he sits among the excellent—that is, among the choice gods.
He is the one who dwells in *ṛta*; that is, he dwells in *ṛta*, which is truth or sacrifice (*yajña*).
He is the one who dwells in the sky; that is, he dwells in the sky, the ether (*vyoman*).
He is born from the waters; that is, he is born in the waters in the form of conchs, shells, mother-of-pearl, sea-monsters, and so forth.

"Born of the cow" means he is born from the earth (*gavi pṛthivyām*) in the form of rice, barley, and so forth; "born of the *ṛta*" means he is born in the form of a constituent of the sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*);
"born of the mountain" means he is born from the mountains in the form of rivers and so forth.
Although he is the self of all, he is indeed *ṛta*, having a nature that is non-false.
He is "vast" (*bṛhat*), meaning great, because he is the cause of everything.
Even when the Sun itself is spoken of in the mantra, there is no contradiction in the Brahmana's explanation, since the Sun is accepted as being of the very nature of the Self.
The meaning of the mantra is that the Self of the universe is one alone, all-pervading, and there is no plurality of selves.
He leads the breath upward; he casts the downward breath inward.
All the gods worship the Dwarf seated in the middle.
The sign for the realization of the true nature of the Self is stated: he who leads the prāṇa—the vital breath or the function of prāṇa—upward from the heart, causing it to go upwards;
and likewise, who casts the apāna downward, i.e., throws it down, such is the completion of the sentence.
Him, seated in the middle within the space of the lotus of the heart, who manifests the light of discernment (*vijñāna*) in the intellect, one should know as the dwarf (*vāmana*).

The meaning is that all the gods—the vital breaths such as sight and the rest—desirable and worthy of worship, bring offerings consisting of the cognition of forms and so forth, and serve him just as subjects serve a king; that is to say, they remain engaged in their respective functions for his sake.
He is the one for whose sake and by whose impulsion all the activities of the organs of air (the vital breaths) proceed.
Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that he is another perfected one (siddha).
When this embodied being, whose body is falling apart and who is being released from the physical frame, what remains here?
This indeed is that. KaU 5.4.2, 2.4.

Furthermore, regarding this Self residing in the body, as it is falling away, as it is departing—the meaning of the word "falling away" is explained by the phrase "being released from the body. What remains here? Nothing at all remains here in the body within the collection of vital breaths and so forth, just as when the master of a house has fled.

Like that of travelers staying in a lodging, at the mere moment of the arrival of the Self, all this—the entire collection of effects and instruments—becomes deprived of its power, shattered, and destroyed; he is the other, the perfected Self.
No mortal lives by means of the out-breath (prāṇa) or the in-breath (apāna);
rather, they live by something else upon which these two are supported.

It might be thought: "This [body] is destroyed only through the departure of the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the in-breath (*apāna*), and so forth, and not through the departure of a self distinct from them; for it is by means of the breaths alone that a mortal lives here.
This is not so.
No mortal man possessing a body lives by means of the out-breath, nor by the in-breath, nor by the eye and other such [faculties]; no one at all lives [by these].
For it is not possible for these [organs], which act for the sake of another, to be the cause of life on the grounds that they function through combination;

for in the world, the continued existence of combined things—such as houses and the like—is never seen to occur unless they are employed by some other entity that acts for its own sake and is not itself a combination.
Therefore, since the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest are likewise combinations, the same must hold true for them as well.
Therefore, by means of that which is distinct from the combined [group] of breath and so forth—indeed, by that very one—all these, being combined, live; they sustain their vital breaths.
When that supreme Self, who is distinct from the combined, exists, these two, prāṇa and apāna, together with the eyes and other organs, depend upon Him.

The intention is this: for the sake of that uncombined One, the combined group remains engaged in all its various activities such as prāṇa, apāna, and so on; thus, He is established as other than them.
Come, I shall declare to you this secret, eternal Brahman,
and how the self becomes [after] reaching death, O Gautama.
Now, O Gautama, I shall again declare to you this secret, hidden, eternal, and ancient Brahman;
through the knowledge of which there is a cessation of all transmigration,
and through the ignorance of which one meets death— listen to how the Self is, and how the Self transmigrates.
Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a physical body;
others pass into stationary objects, according to their karma and according to their learning.
Others—certain ignorant and deluded embodied beings (*dehin*) endowed with the seed of semen—enter the womb, that is, the gateway to the womb, for the sake of taking on a body;
the meaning is that they enter the womb.
Still others, who are extremely base, follow after death toward the state of stationary existence, such as trees and the like; that is, they go toward becoming a stump.

"According to their karma" (*yathākarma*) means that whatever karma they have performed in this life—by the power of that; and likewise "according to what was heard" (*yathāśruta*), meaning they obtain a body exactly corresponding to the kind of knowledge (*vijñāna*) they have acquired. This is because another Vedic text states: "For births [occur] according to one's wisdom" (*yathāprajñaṃ hi saṃbhavāḥ*). (KaU Bh 5.7/2, 2.7)
This person who remains awake while others sleep, fashioning desire after desire—that indeed is the radiant, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal.
Upon it all worlds are supported; no one ever transcends it.
This indeed is that. KaU 5.8.2, 2.8.
He speaks of that secret Brahman which was promised as "I shall declare": "That which remains awake while these [senses], such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), are asleep; it does not sleep.
How so?
By means of ignorance (*avidyā*), it fashions each and every desired object, such as women and the like."
The person who brings about wakefulness—that alone is the bright, radiant, and pure Brahman; there is no other secret Brahman.
That alone is called the immortal and indestructible in all the scriptures.
Moreover, all the worlds, beginning with the earth, are supported—that is, dependent—upon that very Brahman, because He is the cause of all the worlds.
"No one transcends That," and so forth, is exactly as explained previously.

Just as fire, though one, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form, so too the single inner self of all beings assumes a form corresponding to every form, both within and without. (KaU 5.9)

Because the realization of the oneness of the Self—even though established by valid means of knowledge—is not firmly established in the minds of those Brahmins whose internal organs are agitated by the false intellects of many logicians and who possess crooked understandings, despite being taught repeatedly, the Śruti speaks again and again with great care to demonstrate it: "Just as fire, though one alone and consisting of light, illuminates the world... (bhuvanaṃ bhāvayati).
"Bhuvana" means that which contains beings; it refers to this world. Having entered this, he has "entered after" (anupraviṣṭaḥ).
"Pratirūpa" means having a form corresponding to each individual form—that is, with respect to various objects to be burned, such as wood and so forth.
Thus, being "pratirūpa," he became manifold in those various places according to the different things to be burned.

In this very way, the Inner Self of all beings is one alone; being the Self within all beings, it has become a "counter-form" (pratirūpa) for every form because of its extreme subtlety and because it has entered into every body, like [fire] in wood and other materials, while externally it exists in its own unmodified nature like space.

Just as the one wind, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form, so too the single inner self of all beings assumes a form corresponding to every form, both within and without. (KaU 5.10)
Likewise, there is another illustration: "As the wind, though one," and so forth.
Having entered into bodies by means of the self as vital breath (*prāṇa*), he became the counterpart of every form; the rest is the same [as previously explained].

Just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not defiled by external ocular defects, so the one Inner Self of all beings, being external [to them], is not defiled by the suffering of the world. (KaU 5.11)

If it were argued that because the One is the self of all, the suffering of transmigratory existence would belong to the Supreme Being alone, this is said in reply: Just as the sun, while benefiting the eye with its light, is not tainted by the internal defects of sin arising from the sight of impurities such as urine and feces—even though it is the eye for all people who see those things—so too is the Self. By making manifest the impurities of urine, feces, and so forth, it does not become defiled by the internal faults of sin caused by the perception of such impurities, even while being the eye for the entire world that perceives them.

Just as a single entity is not tainted by external defects such as contact with impurities, so too the Inner Self of all beings, being external [to them], is not smeared by the suffering of the world.
For the world experiences suffering arising from desire and action through ignorance superimposed upon its own self;
yet that [suffering] does not exist in the self from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Just as the snake, silver, water, and impurity in a rope, a mother-of-pearl shell, saline soil, and the sky do not exist as defects inherent to the rope and so forth,
yet they are perceived as possessing those defects due to the cause of superimposition through erroneous cognition upon the objects with which they are in contact;
nor are they stained by those defects, for they are external to that erroneous superimposition.

In the same way, the entire world, having superposed upon the Self—which is like the rope—a distorted cognition consisting of action, agent, and fruit (which is like the snake), experiences the suffering of birth, death, and so forth caused by that [superposition].
However, the Self, though being the Self of all the world, is not tainted by the suffering of the world through the cause of such distorted superposition;
for it is external, just like the rope, being outside the range of the superposition of distorted cognition.
The one controller, the inner self of all beings, who makes his single form manifold—those wise ones who perceive him abiding within themselves attain eternal happiness, and no others. (KaU 5.12)
Moreover, He is indeed the Supreme Lord, omnipresent, independent, and one; there is no other equal to Him or superior to Him.
He is the controller, for this entire world exists under His control.
Why? Because He is the inner self (antarātman) of all beings.

Since he makes that very one, the Self— which is of a single essence, pure in the form of consciousness— into many diverse forms by virtue of the distinctions of impure limiting adjuncts such as name and form, through his own mere existence and his inconceivable power; [he is] "situated in the Self," meaning manifested in the form of consciousness within the intellect (buddhi) in the space of the heart of one's own body.
For the self does not have the body as its substratum,
because it is formless like space;
just as in the case of the expression, "the face situated in the mirror."

For those wise and discerning ones who— having turned away from external functions— behold this very Self as the Lord, and directly experience Him in accordance with the instructions of the teacher and the scriptures; for those who have become the Supreme Lord, there arises eternal and constant bliss characterized by the joy of the Self.

It is not so for others—those whose intellects are attached to external things and who lack discrimination—for them, even though it is their own self, it remains hidden due to the intervention of ignorance.
He is the eternal among the transient, the conscious among the conscious, the one who ordains the desires of the many.
Those wise ones who perceive Him abiding within themselves attain eternal peace, and no others. (KaU 5.13)
Furthermore, He is eternal and indestructible among all things that are impermanent and subject to destruction;

He is consciousness among all conscious beings, such as Brahmā and other living creatures. Just as the power to burn belongs only to fire and not to water and other elements, the capacity for volition in others exists solely because of His own self-consciousness.

Moreover, He is omniscient and the Lord of all; by Himself and without effort, He fulfills the desires of many transmigrating beings who possess longing, according to their respective karma—both the fruits of their actions and those desires granted through His own grace.
"It bestows" means "it grants.

For those wise ones who perceive that [bliss] as abiding within themselves, there shall be eternal, perpetual peace—cessation that has become their very own self—but not for others who do not know it thus.
Regarding this, they consider it to be the supreme, indefinable bliss.
How indeed may I understand that? What is it that shines or blazes forth?

That bliss of self-realization— which is indescribable, impossible to describe, supreme, most excellent, and though beyond the reach of the speech and mind of ordinary men— is nevertheless regarded by those Brahmins who have turned away from all desires as being directly perceived; how indeed, in what manner, may I come to know that bliss?
"May I bring this within the range of my own cognition, just as ascetics whose desires have ceased do.
What is it that shines and blazes, being of the nature of light, from which [it follows] whether or not it shines forth clearly and is seen as an object of our cognition? // KaUBh_5.14/2,1.14 //
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire.
It is only after Him, as He shines, that everything shines; by His light all this is illumined.
To this, the following answer appears: "It shines and it illumines.
How so? In that [Brahman], which is one's own self, even the sun—the illuminator of all—does not shine; the meaning is that it does not illuminate that Brahman.
Likewise, neither the moon nor the stars [shine].
These lightnings do not shine;
how much less this fire within the range of our vision?
What need for more? Whatever shines here, beginning with all this, it shines only by following the shining, the blazing, of that Supreme Lord himself.
Likewise, just as water or a firebrand, through contact with fire, burns along with the burning fire but not by itself,
so too does all this— the sun and the rest— shine by its light, that is, its radiance. Since this is so, that very Brahman both shines and illuminates.
Through its various manifestations in its effects, the luminous nature of that Brahman is understood by itself;

for a manifestation that does not exist by itself is not capable of producing the manifestation of another. This is because jars and the like are never seen to be illuminators of other things, whereas luminous entities such as the sun and so forth are seen to possess that quality. (KaU Bh 5.15)
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth Vallī of the Kaṭhavallī.
Now begins the sixth chapter (vallī).

Just as in the world the determination of the root of a tree is accomplished by the very determination of its tuft [of leaves], so too this sixth chapter is commenced with the desire to determine the true nature of the Brahman, which is the root of that tree consisting of the effects of saṃsāra, by means of determining that very tree.
Rooted above and branching below is this eternal Ashvattha tree.
That indeed is the Radiant, that is Brahman, and that alone is called the Immortal.
Upon it all worlds are supported; no one transcends it.
This indeed is that. KaU 6.1/2,3.1.
"Rooted above": that whose root is above is this very tree of saṃsāra, beginning with the unmanifest (avyakta) and ending with the stationary (sthāvara), which has its root in Viṣṇu’s supreme abode.
It is called a "tree" because it is subject to being cut down;

it consists of manifold misfortunes such as uninterrupted birth, old age, death, and grief, and its nature changes at every moment, like a magical illusion, a mirage, water in a desert, or a city of the Gandharvas.

Because its nature is seen and then lost, and because it is non-existent at its end like a tree, it is insubstantial like the trunk of a plantain tree; it is the locus for the conceptual constructions of the minds of hundreds of various heretics, whose true nature remains undetermined by those seeking to know reality; its essential core is determined by the Vedānta to be rooted in the Supreme Brahman; it originates from the seed of ignorance, desire, and karma in their unmanifest state;

it has Hiraṇyagarbha as its sprout, who consists of the two powers of knowledge and action belonging to the Lower Brahman; and it has the differentiation of the subtle bodies (liṅga) of all living beings as its trunk.

That [tree], its pride nourished by the sprinkling of the water of craving; having the sprouts of the objects of the sense-faculties as its shoots, the instruction of the sciences of *śruti*, *smṛti*, and logic as its leaves, and sacrifices, charity, austerity, and various rites as its many flowers; possessing the many flavors of the sensations of pleasure and pain, and yielding infinite fruits upon which living beings subsist;
its roots grown dense and firmly bound by the sprinkling of the water of craving; and its nests built by the birds that are the elements beginning with Brahmā and the worlds beginning with Satyaloka.

This great tree of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-vṛkṣa*), which has become tumultuous with many sounds such as dancing, singing, instrumental music, shouting, clapping, laughing, crying out, wailing "Hā hā!", and "Leave me! Leave me!", arising from the joy and sorrow produced by the pleasure and pain of living beings— this *aśvattha* tree, whose nature is eternally agitated by the winds of desire and action like a horse-fig tree, is cut down by the weapon of the realization of the Self as Brahman, as enjoined in the Vedāntas.
With branches consisting of heaven, hell, animals, pretas, and so forth, it has branches hanging downward;
it is eternal because it is beginningless and has been in existence for a long time.

That which is the root of this tree of saṃsāra is itself the *śukram*—the bright, pure, luminous essence whose nature is the light of consciousness, the self-luminosity; that alone is Brahman, because of its absolute greatness.

That very [Brahman] is called and described as "immortality" because its nature is indestructible and it is the Truth. All else—the modification which is a mere beginning of speech, a name, and unreal—is mortal. In that Brahman, the ultimate reality, all worlds—equal to a city of Gandharvas, a mirage, water in a desert, or a magical illusion—resting upon one another, are entirely dependent during their origination, maintenance, and dissolution, due to the absence of the perception of the ultimate reality.
Therefore, no modification whatsoever—just as a product such as a jar does not transcend or go beyond its material cause such as clay—transcends or goes beyond that Brahman.
This indeed is that.
Whatever exists in this entire world, having issued forth, trembles because of the vital breath (prāṇa).
A great terror, a raised thunderbolt—it is they who know this that become immortal.
As for the claim that "by knowing which one becomes immortal," and that the very root of the world does not exist because this [world] has issued forth from a non-existent Brahman— that is not so;
for whatever exists here, whatever this entire world is, it is all in Prāṇa.
In the Supreme Brahman, which is Truth, everything stirs and trembles;
from Him alone it has issued forth and emerged, and thus it moves and acts according to fixed law.
That Brahman, who is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe, is the Great Terror.
It is "great fear" because it is both great and one fears it;
it is like a raised thunderbolt, as if a thunderbolt were actually uplifted.
Just as servants, upon seeing their master facing them with a thunderbolt raised in his hand, invariably abide by his command, so too [does one abide by the Buddha's teaching].
Thus, it is stated that this world—characterized by the moon, sun, planets, lunar mansions, stars, and so forth—along with its Lord, proceeds according to fixed laws, never resting for even a moment.
Those who know this—that the one Brahman is the witness of the activity of their own self—become immortal, possessing the nature of immortality.
Out of fear of him the fire burns; out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra and Vāyu, and Death as the fifth, run on.
To explain how the world exists out of fear of Him, he says: "Out of fear of this Supreme Lord, fire burns;
out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra, Vāyu, and Death as the fifth run about."

And in this case, if while still living he is able— if being capable— he understands, that is, realizes and comprehends this cause of fear, Brahman, then prior to the dissolution, the falling away, or the disintegration of the body, he is liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra;
but if he was not able to understand it—

Then, due to lack of understanding, it becomes fit—that is, it becomes capable—for the state of having a body, for the sake of a body, within those "creations" (sarga); "creations" refers to the worlds such as the earth in which living beings to be created are produced;
the meaning is that it takes on a body.
Therefore, prior to the dissolution of the body, one must not remain without the realization of the Self;
for it is here alone that the perception of the Self is clearly possible, like the reflection of a face in a mirror, and not in other worlds— except for the world of Brahmā—
and even that is difficult to attain.
How so? It is said:
"As in a mirror, so in the self; as in a dream, so in the world of the ancestors;
as if clearly seen in water, so in the world of the Gandharvas; as in shadow and light, so in the world of Brahman. (KaU 6.5)

Just as the world perceives its own self as a reflection in a mirror, which is utterly distinct [from the mirror], so too here, when one's own intellect has become stainless like a mirror, there occurs the vision of the self as something distinct; this is the meaning.
Just as in a dream, that which is undifferentiated arises from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state.
Likewise, in the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), the vision of the self is indeed indistinct, because of its attachment to the enjoyment of the fruits of karma;

and just as in water one's own form appears as if its parts were indistinct— as if it were being seen all around— in the same way, in the world of the Gandharvas, the vision of the self is indeed indistinct.
And thus, even regarding other worlds, it is understood through the authority of the scriptures that [the two] are utterly distinct from one another,
like shadow and light, within the single Brahma-world alone;
and that world is difficult to attain because it is to be accomplished through exceptionally distinguished karma and knowledge.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that one must exert effort here and now for the sake of realizing the Self.
Having understood the distinctness of the senses, as well as their arising and passing away,
the wise man does not grieve when they arise separately.

How is this to be understood, and what is the purpose of its realization? It is said: [it is the understanding] that the sense organs, such as hearing and the rest, which arise separately from their respective causes—ether and so forth—for the purpose of grasping their own respective objects, possess a state of separation from the utterly pure, absolute nature of the Self consisting of consciousness alone, and thus have a character distinct from their own essential nature.

Likewise, having understood through discrimination that the rising and setting—the birth and dissolution—of those very sense organs occur in relation to the states of waking and dreaming, and do not pertain to the Self, the wise person does not grieve;
for since the Self possesses a single, eternal nature that is never subject to change, it is impossible for it to be the cause of grief.
Accordingly, another Śruti says: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3).

Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect (sattva); higher than the intellect is the Great Self (mahān ātmā); and higher than the Great is the Unmanifest (avyakta). KaU 6.7/2,3.7.
Since the distinctness of the self from the senses has been stated, that [self] is not to be apprehended externally; for it is the inner self (pratyagātman) of everything.
To explain how this is so, it is said: "The mind is superior to the senses," and so forth.
Here, because objects belong to the same class as the senses, they are included by the very mention of the senses.
The rest is as before;
here, by the word "sattva," the intellect (buddhi) is meant. (KaUBh 6.7/2, 3.7)
But beyond the unmanifest is the pervasive Puruṣa, who is indeed without marks;
by knowing him, a living being is liberated and attains immortality.

But the Puruṣa is beyond the unmanifest; he is all-pervasive, and because he is the cause of everything—even of all-pervasive things like space—he is "without marks" (aliṅga). That by which something is marked or understood is a "mark" (liṅga), such as the intellect and so forth; since that does not exist in him, he is indeed without marks.
This refers to being "devoid of all saṃsāric phenomena.
Having learned this from both the teacher and the scripture, a living being is liberated even while alive from the heart-knots of ignorance and so forth;
and upon the falling away of the body, one attains immortality.
"He is without marks, beyond the unmanifest, the Puruṣa"—this is to be connected with what precedes.
His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees him with the eye. He is fashioned by the heart, by intuition, and by the mind; those who know this become immortal. (KaU 6.9)

How, then, is the perception of that signless [reality] possible? It is said: being non-existent, it does not abide within the domain of vision as an object of seeing; such is the nature of this inner self (*pratyagātman*).
Therefore, it is not perceived by the eye or by any of the senses—the mention of the "eye" being intended as an illustration for all the sense organs.
He sees, yet he does not perceive any such thing as this primordial self.
How then is it said that one might see it?—by means of the heart, that is, by the intellect residing in the heart;
by means of "manīṣā," which is the intellect (manīṭ) that governs the mind in its form of volition and so forth, and thus acts as its discriminator.
"By the mind"—that is, by means of the mind in its form of reflection, [namely] right vision (samyag-darśana)—it is "prepared," "accomplished," or "manifested";
the ellipsis of the sentence is that the Self can thus be known. Those who know this Self as Brahman become immortal. (KaU Bh 6.9/2,3.9)
When the five perceptions, together with the mind,
come to rest and the intellect no longer stirs— that, they say, is the supreme goal.

How that mind-stuff which is fixed in the heart is attained— that is the purpose for which yoga is taught: when, at whatever time, the five cognitions— by which the sense organs such as hearing and so forth are called "cognitions" because they have cognition as their purpose— having been withdrawn from their respective objects, abide in the Self alone together with the mind, following it.

By that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which has turned away from volition and the like, the intellect (buddhi)—characterized by determination—does not stir; it does not stir, it does not exert itself in its own functions. They call that the supreme goal.
They consider that steady control of the senses to be yoga;
for at that time one becomes vigilant, since yoga is both the origin and the dissolution.
They consider such a state as "yoga," even though it is actually a state of disjunction;
for this state of the yogi is characterized by the disjunction from the conjunction with all that is harmful.
For in this state, the Self is established in its own true nature, free from the superimpositions of ignorance.
"Firm" means a steady and immovable holding of the senses; that is to say, the steadying of the external and internal organs.
"Vigilant," meaning free from negligence and constantly striving toward concentration—at that time, as is understood by implication, precisely when one has become established in yoga.
For indeed, there is no possibility of negligence when the activities of the intellect and so forth have ceased;
therefore, vigilance is enjoined even before the cessation of the activities of the intellect and so forth.
Or else, it is at the very moment when the steady holding [of the senses] occurs.
At that very moment, there is unrestrained vigilance; therefore, it is said that "he then becomes vigilant.
Why?
Because yoga, by its very nature, is subject to arising and passing away—meaning it is characterized by appearance and disappearance.
Therefore, the intention is that one must practice heedfulness in order to avoid the states of woe.
It cannot be grasped by speech, nor by the mind, nor by the eye;
how can it be perceived otherwise than from one who says, "It exists"? (KaU 6.12)
If this Brahman were an object of activity such as cognition, it would be perceived specifically as "this is that";
however, when cognition and the rest cease, Brahman—being unperceived due to the absence of any means of apprehension—simply does not exist.
For in the world, it is well known that whatever falls within the range of the sense organs exists, while the opposite is non-existent.

Therefore, since [Brahman] is not perceived, the application [of words] is useless, or else one might conclude that it does not exist; thus, when it is reached that Brahman must be perceived, this is said in reply:
"True.
The meaning is that it cannot be attained by speech, nor by mind, nor by the eye, nor even by the other sense organs.
Nevertheless, although it is devoid of all particularities, it certainly exists because it is understood to be the root of the world; for the dissolution of effects culminates in existence.
For indeed, when this effect is traced through a succession of increasingly subtle stages, it leads precisely to the realization of the notion of Being (sat).
Even when the intellect (*buddhi*) is being dissolved through the dissolution of its objects, it dissolves only while still containing within it the cognition of existence (*sat-pratyaya*).
For the intellect is our means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for understanding the true nature of both the existent and the non-existent.
If the root of the world did not exist, this effect, being permeated by non-existence, would be perceived simply as "non-existent."
But this is not the case; rather,
it is perceived as being truly existent,
just as the effects of clay and so forth, such as jars and the like, are permeated by clay and so forth.
Therefore, it must be understood that the self exists as the root of the world.
Why?
Because, apart from one who asserts existence, who follows the meaning of the scriptures, and who possesses faith, there is no one else—namely, the nihilist who says "it does not exist."
When one possesses a perverted view, thinking that there is no root for the world, that the self does not exist, and that this effect is merely without continuity and dissolves into non-existence—
how can that Brahman be perceived in its true reality?
The meaning is that it cannot be perceived in any way whatsoever.
"It exists"—thus indeed should both be perceived through their true nature;
for one who perceives "it exists," the true nature becomes clear.

Therefore, having set aside the demonic position of those who maintain the doctrine of non-existence (*asad-vāda*), the Self should be realized as truly existing through the adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), the effect (*kārya*), and so forth, according to the view that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*sat-kārya*).

However, when the Self is devoid of those adjuncts and is changeless, and when the effect does not exist apart from its cause—as stated in the Śruti: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth" (ChU 6.1.4)—then there occurs the realization of the true nature of that Self, which is free from adjuncts, without marks (*aliṅga*), and beyond the scope of notions such as "existent" or "non-existent."

And the phrase "the Self is to be perceived by means of that form" follows [from the previous context]. There too, regarding both—the qualified (sopādhika) and the unqualified (nirupādhika) states of existence and reality—the genitive case is used for the purpose of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). The meaning is: first, the Self is perceived as simply "existing," having been perceived through the notion of existence produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the pre-existent effect (*satkārya*).

Thereafter, the true nature of the Self— whose form is free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), which is distinct from both the known and the unknown, and whose essence is non-dual— is revealed; as indicated by such scriptural passages as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (BĀU 3.8.8), and "invisible, bodiless, inexpressible, without abode" (TaittU 2.7.1), it becomes serene and manifests itself.
This refers to one who has previously perceived "it exists" for the purpose of self-illumination. (KaUBh 6.13/2,3.13)
When all desires that dwell within his heart are utterly released, then the mortal becomes immortal; even here he attains Brahman.
Thus, for one who perceives the Self as the ultimate reality, at whatever time all desires are liberated— that is, they dissolve— due to the absence of anything else to be desired; |||
Those [desires] which, prior to his awakening, resided—that is, were supported—in the heart, that is, the intellect (*buddhi*) of this wise man;
for the intellect is the substratum of desires, not the Self, as established by another scriptural passage beginning with, "Desire, volition... (BĀU 1.5.3).

Now, that mortal who previously existed before awakening becomes immortal after awakening due to the destruction of death—characterized by ignorance, desire, and action; for when death, which is the cause of movement, is destroyed, movement is no longer possible. Thus, right here, like the extinguishing of a lamp, through the cessation of all bonds, he attains Brahman; the meaning is that he becomes Brahman itself, as it is said:
"When all the knots of the heart are severed here."
Then the mortal becomes immortal; for this is the extent of the instruction.

When, then, is there the destruction of desires at their very root? It is said: when all the knots of the heart—that is, of the intellect—while one is still living here, are split asunder, undergo division, and perish; the meaning is that these are the conditions of ignorance which, like knots, exist in the form of firm bonds.

Characterized by such notions as "I am this body," "this wealth is mine," and "I am happy or miserable," [these desires] perish when the contrary realization of the Self as Brahman arises—namely, "I am indeed Brahman, free from transmigratory existence. When the knots of ignorance are destroyed, the desires caused by them perish at their very root. Then, the mortal becomes immortal; for this is all, this alone, this much and nothing more—such is the doubt that must not be entertained.
"Instruction," "teaching," and "advice" refer to all the Vedāntas; this is the completion of the sentence. (KaUBh 6.15/2, 3.15)
There are one hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upwards by that, one attains immortality; the others lead to departure in various directions.

For the wise one who has become Brahman even while alive—having severed the entire knot of ignorance and the like through the realization of the Self as the all-pervading Brahman from which all distinctions have been cast away—there is no further journey, because it is stated: "Here he attains Brahman," and also from another scriptural passage: "His vital breaths do not depart; being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).

Furthermore, for those who know Brahman only dimly and are devoted to other branches of knowledge— who partake of the world of Brahmā— as well as for those who are the opposite of them and partake of saṃsāra,
it is precisely their specific destinies that are described here, for the purpose of praising the fruit of the preeminent knowledge of Brahman under discussion.
Moreover, the knowledge of the fires (agnividyā) was both asked about and answered.
And since the manner of attaining that fruit must be explained, the commencement of the mantra is made.

In this regard: "A hundred" means a hundred in number, and "one" refers to the channel named Suṣumnā, which has issued forth from the heart of the person; among those vessels (nāḍīs), one named Suṣumnā has emerged, having pierced through the crown of the head.
By means of that [path], having brought the self under control at the time of death, one should unite it with [Brahman].

By that [path], moving upward through the channels and departing by way of the sun, one attains relative immortality—the state of being free from death—as the Smṛti states: "The station until the dissolution of all beings is indeed called immortality" (ViP).
Or, after having experienced incomparable enjoyments in the world of Brahman, one attains primary immortality at a later time along with Brahman.
The other channels, which have various diverse courses in every direction, serve for departing [from the body] and lead only to the attainment of transmigratory existence; this is the meaning.
The Person, the size of a thumb, the inner self, is ever seated in the hearts of men.
One should draw him forth from one's own body with steadfastness, as one extracts the stalk from the *muñja* grass.
One should know him as the bright, the immortal—yes, one should know him as the bright, the immortal.
Now, for the purpose of summarizing the meaning of the entire chapter, he says: "The Person, the inner self, the size of a thumb, is ever seated within the heart of people as previously described;
one should draw him out from one's own body, exert oneself to lift him up, and separate him—this is the meaning.
With what, as it were? It is said: like the inner stalk of Muñja grass, with fortitude and vigilance."
One should know—that is, understand—that pure consciousness (cinmātra) extracted from the body as the bright, pure, immortal Brahman as described above.
The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of concluding the Upaniṣad, and the word "iti" [marks the end]. KaUBh 6.17/2,3.17.

Then Naciketas, having obtained this knowledge proclaimed by Death, as well as the entire method of yoga, attained Brahman, became free from passion, and was released from death; so too shall it be for any other who knows the supreme Self.

Now, this conclusion of the narrative is stated for the purpose of praising the knowledge: "Then, having received"—that is, having obtained—"this entire Brahma-knowledge as proclaimed by Death," meaning exactly as described, together with the method of yoga, along with its accessories and its fruit; this is the meaning of the word *naciketāḥ*. "From Death" means from Yama, the giver of the boons.
What [did he obtain]? He attained Brahman; the meaning is that he became liberated.

How? By the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*), having become free from passion (*virajaḥ*)—meaning devoid of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*)—and free from death, meaning free from desire and ignorance (*kāma-avidyā*).

Not only Naciketas, but whoever else, like Naciketas, is a knower of the Self (*ātmavit*) who has attained the internal Self alone—the unqualified, immediate (*pratyak*) essential nature—the intention is that such a person attains Reality itself (*tattvam*).

There is no other form that is not the inner self; thus, one who knows—that is, understands—the internal self in the manner described becomes free from passion (*virajaḥ*), and having attained Brahman, he becomes immortal; this is the completion of the sentence.
May He protect us both together.
May He protect us both together; may we work together with vigor.
May our study be brilliant; may we never harbor hatred toward one another.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Thus ends the third Vallī in the second Adhyāya of the Kaṭhopaniṣad.

This peace (*śānti*) is spoken for the purpose of pacifying the defects arising from the improper acquisition of knowledge or its imparting through negligence on the part of both disciple and teacher: "May He protect us both together"—who? That very Supreme Lord who has been revealed in the *Upaniṣad* by means of the manifestation of the true nature of knowledge.
Furthermore, "may He nourish us both together," that is, may He protect us by manifesting the fruit thereof.
"Let us two together perform—that is, accomplish—the power and capacity produced by knowledge.
Furthermore, let that which has been studied by us two be brilliant;
or rather, the meaning is: let that which has been studied by us two be exceedingly brilliant and full of vigor."
"Let us not hate one another"—the meaning is that the disciple and the teacher should not harbor hatred toward each other on account of faults arising from negligent or improper study and teaching.
"Peace! Peace! Peace!"—this threefold utterance is for the purpose of pacifying all defects. Om. Thus ends [Kaushītaki Upaniṣad 6.19].

Thus ends the commentary on the Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the wandering ascetic teacher of the supreme order (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya) and the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda.
